book.title: The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail
book.author: Clayton M. Christensen

chapters.title: How Can Great Firms Fail? Insights from the Hard Disk Drive Industry
chapters.hook: The firm that failed had just posted its best quarterly numbers, and every decision that led there was sound.
chapters.counterintuition: Failure looks like negligence from the outside. Inside, it looks like a very good quarter. In fact, the same discipline that sharpens execution in an established market can narrow what that market is allowed to show you.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one type of buyer who never shows up in your customer feedback. Write down what they use instead of your product. That gap is where the next relevant signal lives.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Your current customers define what your business should improve next. That same definition quietly excludes the buyers outside their world, which is where the next market is forming.

breakdown.fastRead:
The product team had a full quarter of customer feedback and every piece of it said the same thing: the current format was exactly right. No major buyer wanted the new one. The performance gap was real, the quality comparison was honest, and the investment case for staying the course was solid. The project was rejected in a meeting that followed good process and reached the wrong conclusion.

Serving your current customers well is not the mistake. It is the mechanism. Resource allocation follows what your best buyers will pay for, which means it also points away from what your best buyers cannot yet use.

What they cannot tell you is where the market is forming that will replace them.
breakdown.deepRead:
The hard disk drive industry ran through product generations so quickly that researchers used it the way biologists use fruit flies: the cycle was short enough to observe complete. Over two decades, market leadership transferred multiple times. Not because the leaders stopped improving. Because they improved exactly what their current buyers wanted.

Each generation brought better capacity, speed, and reliability. The companies that led each generation had earned their position by doing precisely that. The problem emerged when a new form factor appeared that offered worse performance on every dimension the leading customers cared about, but served a market the leaders barely noticed. Smaller drives were cheaper, used less power, and fit into portable computers that enterprise buyers considered peripheral. No data center manager was asking for one. No enterprise account generated a project plan for it. The investment never cleared the resource allocation meeting.

What cleared those meetings was more of what the current customers were already buying. That is not negligence. That is rational resource allocation functioning exactly as designed.

The disk drive market was the closest thing to a controlled lab that business research had found: generations turned fast enough that you could watch a leader vanish in real time. The companies that disappeared were often the most competent operators in the industry. Their customers had simply shaped their line of sight so precisely that the next market was invisible until it was already large.

The mechanism works like this: your budget process is a measuring instrument calibrated to your current customers. Whatever they cannot use does not generate signal. A technology that is unappealing to your top accounts produces zero data on your dashboards: not negative data, not a warning, just silence. Silence gets misread as absence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about what a disciplined customer listening process actually produces. A company that surveys its best buyers, tracks their satisfaction, and funds the improvements they request is doing what good management requires. The feedback is real. The investment follows the feedback. The product improves in exactly the ways the customers specified.

What the feedback cannot contain is the preferences of buyers who are not yet in the room. A buyer who has not adopted the category cannot describe what would make it right for them. A market that does not yet have a name cannot fill out a survey. So a well-run feedback process produces a faithful picture of the existing market and a blank page where the next market sits.

Consider what Camille's expansion dashboard showed her. Revenue per location was rising. Renewal rates tracked above baseline. Customer satisfaction held quarter over quarter. Every metric that had predicted success in the previous six markets was pointing in the same direction for the next three. The committee approval was correct given what the dashboard measured. The dashboard was correct given the customers it measured. Each link in the chain was sound, and the chain led somewhere the dashboard could not describe.

You probably have a version of this. Not for a video rental operation. Maybe for a product line, a service tier, or a client segment that generates strong numbers right now. Ask which buyers are generating signal in your measurement system. Then ask which buyers are not. The absent ones are not necessarily the most important buyers for the next decade. They might be. Your measurement system cannot tell you either way.

The usual objection to all of this is that companies cannot chase every possible market and must focus on what generates revenue. That objection is correct, and the argument here is not against it. The argument is not that incumbents should stop serving their profitable customers. It is narrower: a company whose investment decisions are made entirely by signals from profitable customers will systematically miss the opportunities that profitable customers cannot describe. Discipline applied to the present is the right tool for managing the present. Applied as the only tool for assessing the future, it produces a structural blind spot: not a character flaw, not a failure of nerve, but a systematic gap between what the current measurement instruments can reach and what is forming beyond them.

Here is the practical version. Your best customers are giving you the most accurate map of where you already are. The non-customer, the buyer who finds your product too expensive, too complex, or simply irrelevant to their situation, is not a lost prospect. They are the outline of the next network. They cannot tell you what it will look like. They can tell you that it is forming somewhere beyond them.

Good management applied to the current business is the mechanism, not the solution.

A company can have excellent survey methodology, a well-run budget process, a strong performance culture, and a committed leadership team. It can still produce this outcome reliably, repeatedly, across industries and eras. The failure does not require bad decisions. It requires only that the decisions stay inside the frame the current customers define.

examples.title: Charlotte Uses Advertiser Feedback to Shelve the Digital Column
examples.scenario: Charlotte has already set down her coffee when the agency buyer slides the rate card back across the table. "We're not sending any budgets there," he says. The weekly advertiser review is spread in front of her: six pages of print performance data, one narrow column at the far right showing forty-two digital classified listings last week against nine hundred in the same print section. Every significant buyer in the room is a print buyer. Every one of them has said the same thing. Charlotte must decide whether to take their consensus back to the product team as evidence that the digital investment proposal should be shelved.
examples.whatToDo: Ask which advertisers are not in the room and what they are using instead. The buyers at the table are telling you the truth about the current product. They cannot tell you anything about the next buyer base.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback from current profitable advertisers accurately describes what current profitable advertisers need. It produces no information about the category of buyers forming outside the room who do not yet use your product.

examples.title: James Takes the Franchise Scores to the Investment Committee
examples.scenario: Performance reports on three-hole paper, fanned across the board table in order of franchise revenue. James checks the top line before the chair sits down. The seven highest-performing franchises are all in the room. None of them use the online booking pilot. All of them have said the same thing about it: their clients call. James is presenting the pilot's twelve-month results to a committee where the franchisees he most relies on have already made clear that the tool does not serve their customers, and their satisfaction scores are the highest in the chain.
examples.whatToDo: Track the customers who are booking through channels the committee never sees. Feedback from top franchisees accurately describes top-franchisee customers and produces a blind spot everywhere else.
examples.whyItMatters: The franchisees who are loudest in the investment committee are the ones who generate the most revenue, so their signal dominates. What goes unmeasured is whether a different type of buyer would use a channel those franchisees have already dismissed.

examples.title: David's Survey Finds No Threat from Digital Cameras
examples.scenario: At 9:15 a.m. Thursday, David opens the competitive analysis. The quality comparison matrix covers grain resolution, color saturation, and cost per image. Film wins on all three columns. The professional photographer survey sampled 200 working photographers: none of them would consider digital for client work at current quality levels. The market-entry recommendation on page twelve says hold position. David must decide whether to accept the analysis as written or ask why the survey only sampled professional photographers.
examples.whatToDo: Commission a separate study covering buyers who do not currently use film cameras at all. The survey proved what professional photographers need. It produced no information about what a different category of buyer might accept.
examples.whyItMatters: A survey that samples only the current customer base confirms the current product's position accurately and generates no information about the next buyer base. The recommendation is correct for the audience it surveyed.

examples.title: Camille's Dashboard Approves the Seventh Market
examples.scenario: It took Camille three expansion cycles to see what the dashboard had been hiding from her. The prediction model had worked six times: revenue per location rising, renewal rates strong, satisfaction scores above baseline. The committee was about to approve the seventh expansion without a dissenting vote. Camille would later trace the gap to what the model never tracked: not the loyal weekly visitors who generated the revenue signal, but the casual users who had stopped coming without ever registering as a departure.
examples.whatToDo: Before approving the next expansion, run a separate count of inactive accounts from the previous two years. Strong engagement from core users can mask a contracting casual base if the dashboard only measures customers who show up.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue metrics track the customers who are currently active. They do not track customers who used to be active and are no longer. A shrinking casual base looks like silence on a dashboard built for loyal users.

examples.title: Henrik's Postmortem Explains the Correct Decision
examples.scenario: The arrivals lane is empty at 11:18 p.m. and has been for forty minutes. Henrik's postmortem for the board is on the table: the contract renewal had been the right decision. Corporate account satisfaction ran at ninety-two percent. Concierge partnership renewals were confirmed. The airport authority had extended on the basis of service metrics no other operator could match. Henrik must now explain to the board why dispatch volume has dropped eighteen percent over the same period that the satisfaction scores were climbing.
examples.whatToDo: Map who is not captured in the corporate account data. The satisfaction metrics describe service to accounts that use the contract. They say nothing about the travelers who used to take taxis before finding a different option.
examples.whyItMatters: A contract built on enterprise accounts measures enterprise account satisfaction accurately. The private passenger who has stopped showing up does not generate a complaint. They simply disappear from the data without registering as a departure.

examples.title: Yusuf Approves the Largest Print Run in a Decade
examples.scenario: You have just signed off on the largest print run in the company's history. Yusuf's annual review shows record institutional sales driven by school district upgrades, and the pipeline for next year is solid. The before looks like a peak: strong demand, healthy margins, a waiting list for the deluxe edition. The after arrives four years later, when the upgrade cycle ends and the districts that drove the record year are not replacing at the same cadence. The demand was real. It was also the last strong expression of a purchasing pattern that was already shifting.
examples.whatToDo: Identify which customers drove the record and whether their demand is structural or tied to a replacement cycle. A strong year powered by institutional upgrades tells you less about future demand than a strong year driven by first-time buyers.
examples.whyItMatters: Institutional buyers on upgrade cycles can produce strong demand metrics that look like stable market strength. The difference between structural demand and cycle-driven demand is invisible inside a single year of sales data.

questions.prompt: The product line has high satisfaction scores from its top accounts and strong renewal rates. The leadership team uses this data to argue against investing in a simpler, lower-cost version. What is the clearest gap in this reasoning?
choices: The data describes existing buyers accurately but produces no information about potential buyers who find the current product too expensive or too complex to use.

High satisfaction scores from the top accounts are a reliable indicator of retention within those accounts but produce no signal about the pricing or complexity barriers that keep other potential buyers from entering the market.

The leadership team should develop the simpler version based on the cost structure of the existing product line, because lower-cost production would allow the company to serve both the premium segment and the entry-level segment from the same platform.
questions.explanation: Current buyer satisfaction data is accurate about current buyers. It cannot describe buyers who are not yet in the system. Using it to reject a product they might adopt is a structural omission, not a measurement error.

questions.prompt: When a dispatch company renews a major airport contract after reporting ninety-two percent satisfaction from its corporate accounts, total dispatch volume has fallen eighteen percent over the same period. Which conclusion best explains the gap?
choices: The satisfaction survey used a flawed methodology, and the proper approach would be to separate account-level satisfaction from total service volume trends.

Corporate account satisfaction and total dispatch volume measure different populations: the first captures clients who stayed, while the second reflects trends among all travelers including those who stopped using the service.

Aggregated dispatch volume tracks customer sentiment across the full service population with less sampling bias than account-level surveys, so the eighteen percent drop in total volume should be weighted as the primary indicator rather than deferring to segment-level satisfaction scores.
questions.explanation: A satisfaction metric built on enterprise accounts captures enterprise account satisfaction precisely. It produces no signal from private travelers who stopped using taxis without registering a complaint anywhere in the system.

questions.prompt: The film camera manufacturer surveys two hundred working photographers about a new digital format. Ninety percent say they would not switch from film at current quality levels. What does this finding tell the company, and what does it fail to tell?
choices: The finding accurately reflects that working photographers already invested in film workflows are not the first target market for the new format, making commercial viability among current film users the appropriate conclusion to draw from this sample.

The finding accurately records the preferences of photographers whose work depends on film's current quality characteristics, making their negative response the strongest available indicator of the technology's current performance gap relative to professional workflows.
The finding accurately describes the preferences of working photographers but produces no information about buyers who do not currently use professional cameras at all.
questions.explanation: Sampling current professional users confirms what current professional users need. The survey design excludes the buyer who uses a camera occasionally, or not at all, and who might find the digital format's tradeoffs acceptable. That buyer is absent from the data, not absent from the market.

questions.prompt: The franchise chain's highest-revenue locations report that they do not need an online booking platform because their clients prefer phone-based reservations. A planning committee uses this feedback to reject the platform investment. What is the most important unexamined question?
choices: The high-revenue franchises are incorrect about their own customers and need independent audits to validate the preferences they reported.
Customer feedback from profitable franchises dominates the committee's signal while the behavior of buyers outside those top locations goes unmeasured.

The platform captures structured booking data the phone channel cannot retain, which is what enables the origin-destination segmentation the committee's expansion planning team has been requesting for the current planning cycle.
questions.explanation: The feedback from top franchises is accurate about top-franchise customers. The problem is that the committee's dominant signal comes from the locations most committed to the current model, which creates a systematic gap around buyer types those locations do not serve.

questions.prompt: In the disk drive industry, market leaders kept improving their products for current buyers and repeatedly lost position when new disk drive generations emerged. What explains this pattern?
choices: Each generation's leader improved exactly what current buyers needed, which pointed resources away from the smaller-form products that served a different and initially smaller market.
The leaders were cutting corners on quality to reduce manufacturing costs, which caused their loyal enterprise customers to shift purchases to newer entrants.
The new entrants had larger engineering teams and more R&D investment, which let them iterate faster and overtake incumbents who were underinvesting in smaller form factors.
questions.explanation: Sustaining innovations followed the direction current buyers set. That direction was rational and correct for the current market. It was also the direction away from the form factors that later became the mainstream. The investments made sense; the frame they were made inside was narrowing.

questions.prompt: The expansion model has worked reliably across six markets, generating strong revenue per location, renewal rates, and satisfaction scores. The seventh market produces identical metrics. Which question would reveal whether the model has reached a new population or is re-measuring the same population?
choices: Whether the marketing spend is generating trial from genuinely new population segments or concentrating on the same buyer profiles the model has already captured in the six previous markets.

Whether the satisfaction metrics are capturing the experience of first-time users in the seventh market or drawing primarily on early adopters whose profile closely matches the customers already served in the prior expansions.
Whether the customers generating the strong metrics are the core heavy users or a broader casual base that may be contracting separately.
questions.explanation: A dashboard built on active users measures active users well. It cannot distinguish between a stable total market and a market where casual users are drifting away while core users stay strong. The expansion signal is real; the question is what it is actually measuring.

questions.prompt: An editorial director reports record institutional sales for a print reference product, driven by school district upgrade cycles. The investment committee approves a major new edition on this basis. What does the sales record fail to capture?
choices: Whether the school district upgrade cycle that drove the record year is a recurring multi-year pattern or a one-time capital budget event that the district planning cycle is unlikely to repeat at the same volume.
Whether the demand driving the record year is structural market strength or a one-time cycle that will not repeat at the same volume.
Whether the production pipeline for the next edition has the capacity to meet the demand volume that a repeat of the school district upgrade cycle would require.
questions.explanation: Institutional buyers on replacement cycles can produce peak demand that looks like stable market depth. The upgrade cycle explains the record year. It does not predict what happens when the cohort that just bought completes its cycle.

questions.prompt: A market intelligence director argues that the company is well-protected from competitive threats because it runs the industry's most comprehensive customer satisfaction survey. What is the strongest critique of this position?
choices: The survey methodology samples from active subscribers, which structurally excludes the population that has already left the service, so the loyalty scores the dashboard shows are drawn from a group that has self-selected toward continued engagement rather than representing the full subscriber base.
The director should use net promoter scores instead of satisfaction surveys, which capture both advocates and detractors in the current customer pool more accurately.

A comprehensive survey of current customers produces an accurate picture of the existing market and a blank space where markets not yet served by the company are forming. The comprehensiveness is real; the blind spot is structural.
questions.explanation: The survey is comprehensive within its scope. Its scope is current customers. Buyers who have not yet adopted the category, who find the product too expensive, or who use an alternative that does not appear in the survey simply do not exist in the data. Comprehensive coverage of existing buyers is not comprehensive coverage of the market.

questions.prompt: A product manager concludes that a new technology poses no near-term threat after surveying the top ten accounts and finding that none of them plan to adopt it. Which reasoning error does this commit?
choices: It treats the absence of demand from current top accounts as evidence of no demand from all buyer types, including those not currently in the account base.
It uses account size as the primary filter for evaluating technology threats, which prevents it from detecting adoption patterns among buyers outside the top accounts.
It relies on qualitative feedback rather than quantitative adoption metrics.
questions.explanation: The top accounts are the right people to ask about whether they will adopt the technology. They are not the right people to ask about whether a buyer outside the current account base will adopt it. The survey is correct on its stated population and silent on the next one.

reviewCards.front: Your top accounts just gave you strong feedback that a new product format is not right for them. What should you verify before using that as a reason to kill the project?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the feedback describes the full market or only the current buyer base. Top accounts are telling you the truth about their needs. They cannot tell you what buyers outside their world would accept.

reviewCards.front: A company keeps improving its product for current customers and keeps losing market share to entrants. How is that possible?
reviewCards.back: Improvement follows what current buyers will pay for, which points resources away from the markets entrants can enter first. Serving current buyers well is the mechanism for missing disruptive entrants, not the protection against them.

reviewCards.front: Why was the disk drive industry useful as a research case for studying how great firms fail?
reviewCards.back: Product generations cycled so quickly that the pattern of leadership transfer could be observed in real time rather than over decades. The same mechanism visible elsewhere over a generation played out in years.

reviewCards.front: A company runs strong customer satisfaction scores while total dispatch volume falls. What are the two things being measured differently?
reviewCards.back: Satisfaction scores measure the customers who are still actively using the service. Volume measures all travelers, including those who stopped using the service without registering a complaint. The two populations are not the same.

reviewCards.front: What does 'serving current customers well' prevent a company from seeing?
reviewCards.back: It filters out signal from buyers outside the current value network: buyers who won't pay the same price, don't need the same performance, or use a different channel the company has not built for.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to separate what your current customer feedback can measure from what it cannot, and to treat that gap as a real signal rather than an absence of data.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing customer satisfaction data
ifThenPlans.plan: If satisfaction is strong across top accounts, then also pull a count of inactive or lapsed accounts from the same period and ask what those users are doing instead.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new product proposal
ifThenPlans.plan: If the evaluation team is made up of people serving current customers, then add one explicit question: who would use this at lower quality, and what would they trade away to do so?

ifThenPlans.context: approving an expansion or investment
ifThenPlans.plan: If the investment case rests on customer feedback, then identify which buyers are generating that feedback and whether a different type of buyer would reach a different conclusion.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing competitive intelligence
ifThenPlans.plan: If a competitor is growing in a segment you do not serve, treat their customer base as a signal about what your current measurement instruments cannot reach.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one buyer type that has no voice in your most recent product or investment decision. Write one sentence about what that buyer would say about your product if asked today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, identify one customer who is not in your measurement system and find out what they use instead of your product. Track that list for a month.

chapters.title: Value Networks and the Impetus to Innovate
chapters.hook: The product that failed your quality review this morning may be exactly what someone else's market has been waiting for.
chapters.counterintuition: When you evaluate a new product against your current standards and reject it, even though the rejection is correct for your market, you may be wrong about another one. The quality test you trust is calibrated to the network you already serve.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one product or service you recently rejected for not meeting your standards. Write one sentence about what a customer in a different market would find useful about it at exactly this level of quality.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A value network defines what your organization considers worth building. A product that fails inside one network may be exactly right inside another.

breakdown.fastRead:
The benchmark comparison had eight rows. Precision accuracy, simulation fidelity, mesh resolution, processing speed, error tolerance, documentation format, API compatibility, and licensing structure. The simplified product failed six of them. The product director showed the table at the quarterly review and the room agreed: this product did not belong in the roadmap.

The aerospace engineers who generated that table were right about what aerospace engineering requires. The problem is that the table was only ever calibrated to one kind of work.

A value network defines what matters. Your current customers shape that definition, and it becomes your measuring instrument for everything.
breakdown.deepRead:
A value network is not just your customer segment. It is the full set of rules your market applies to decide what is worth building. The rules live in your margin requirements, your product specifications, your sales process, the customers who set your planning calendar, and the improvements they will pay for. Everything in that system points in a consistent direction. Projects that fit the direction get funded. Projects that don't produce no signal: not a vote against, just silence.

This is why the same product can fail one evaluation room and succeed in another. The standards that govern the evaluation are different. In one network, precision is load-bearing: if the simulation is not accurate to four decimal places, the customer will not certify the result. In another network, good enough at low cost is the whole point. A maker community running a small-batch prototype does not care whether the tool runs at aerospace tolerances. The simplified product was genuinely inferior to the flagship in the first network and genuinely useful in the second. Both assessments were correct. They were correct about different things.

Resource allocation follows profit logic. Your business funds what your best customers will pay for because that is where the return is clear and the criteria are legible. A new product that serves a different network has a structural problem: the criteria for evaluating it do not exist inside your planning process. It will be judged by your network's rules, fail them, and disappear from the roadmap.

That actual market has no vote in your budget meeting.

The impetus to innovate, the pull that drives where R&D goes, comes from your current customers. What they want more of gets funded. What they cannot use generates no pull. A disruptive product entering from another network does not look dangerous at first. It looks weak. It looks like it failed the review.
breakdown.fullRead:
Consider what an evaluation against current standards actually does. When you run a new product through your quality checklist, you are asking whether it serves your market at your market's requirements. That is the right question for managing the current business. It is not the right question for assessing whether the product has any market at all.

Etienne's compliance checklist for aviation maintenance software had twelve required fields. Every commercial airline he served required all twelve. The checklist was not bureaucracy: it was a legal and regulatory baseline for an industry where a documentation error could ground a fleet. The checklist was correct. A tablet-based app that skipped six of those fields was not acceptable in that network. The small-aircraft mechanics using the same app in a different context did not need those six fields, had no fleet to ground, and had never heard of the regulatory pathway the airlines required. Neither evaluation was wrong. They were measuring different things.

Here is the practical question: which requirements on your evaluation checklist are universal, and which are specific to the network you already serve?

You probably cannot answer that quickly. Most organizations cannot, because the checklist was assembled from what current customers required and the distinction between those two categories has blurred over time. The blur is not careless. It is the natural result of building an evaluation process inside one network.

The frame of the evaluation is too narrow to show you the other network.

A new product that fits a different network will arrive looking weak by every criterion you have, because your criteria were built for your network. You will see something that fails six of eight quality tests and conclude it is a poor product. It may genuinely be poor for your market. Whether it is poor in its actual market is a different question.

Sophie's postmortem on the credit union lending tool confirmed every step of the original analysis. The loan sizes were below the bank's minimum. The approval criteria were too simple for mid-market commercial underwriting. The documentation trail was too thin. Every decision was correct inside the bank's model. The postmortem recorded no explanation for why the credit union's small-business lending portfolio had grown faster than the bank's over the same period. The bank's model did not have a category for borrowers who were outside the bank's network.

This is what value-network logic does at scale. An organization can run excellent analysis, apply consistent criteria, reach defensible conclusions, and systematically miss the markets forming outside its evaluation frame. The analysis is not flawed. The frame is narrower than the market.

Name the value network you are measuring against right now. Name the one you are not. That is the gap worth closing.

examples.title: Claire's Benchmark Table Has No Row for Hobbyists
examples.scenario: "The error tolerance fails by a factor of twelve," the lead engineer says, turning the benchmark table toward Claire. She has the simplified simulation tool's scores in front of her: aerospace tolerances, mesh resolution, material modeling depth, processing speed under load. The product places last on six of eight measures. The maker community forum where hobbyists are posting projects built with the tool does not appear in the presentation. Claire must decide whether to recommend shelving the tool based on the benchmark results or ask why the benchmark criteria only reflect the requirements of aerospace customers.
examples.whatToDo: Before shelving, identify what criteria the maker community is applying and whether the tool passes those. The benchmark table is accurate for aerospace users. It produces no information about the network where the tool is already being used.
examples.whyItMatters: A benchmark built from current customer requirements will confirm what current customers need. It cannot confirm whether the product has value in a different network applying different standards.

examples.title: Thomas Runs Restaurant Economics on a Home-Baker Kit
examples.scenario: The large-format professional flour sacks are stacked four high. Beside them, the small-batch home-baker kit holds two cups. Thomas runs the unit economics through the restaurant account model: cost per unit, minimum order size, delivery margin per route stop. The home-baker product fails all three. It passes every measure a different kind of customer would apply, but the model for that customer has never been built, and the customer is not in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Run a separate unit economics model calibrated to a direct-to-consumer channel before using the restaurant account model to kill the home-baker line. The restaurant model is accurate for restaurant customers.
examples.whyItMatters: The unit economics that govern the restaurant channel are not universal laws. They reflect what makes business viable in one specific network. A product that fails those economics may be viable in a network with different margin requirements and a different distribution structure.

examples.title: Etienne Declines the App That the Small Shops Already Use
examples.scenario: At 10:40 a.m. Tuesday, Etienne opens the acquisition brief for the tablet-based maintenance app. The compliance audit checklist has twelve required fields. The app covers six. No commercial airline he serves would accept it. The small-aircraft MRO shops using the app daily are not in his customer database, and their requirements are not on the checklist. Etienne must decide whether to pass on the acquisition based on the compliance audit or to ask why the checklist only reflects the requirements of customers who need all twelve fields.
examples.whatToDo: Before closing the file, identify which customers are successfully using the app and what compliance requirements they are operating under. The audit was correct for airline customers. It produced no information about the network where the app is running.
examples.whyItMatters: Compliance requirements are specific to the network they were written for. An app that fails airline compliance may be well-suited to a network where those regulations do not apply. Both facts can be true at the same time.

examples.title: Ingrid's Team Predicts the Right Thing About the Wrong Network
examples.scenario: Which app is worth buying: one that handles twelve routes well, or one that handles three hundred routes poorly? Ingrid's team predicts that the regional transit app will never meet the city system's requirements, and that prediction is technically correct. The app has no payment integration, no accessibility compliance pathway, and no capacity for the city's route complexity. The reveal: the regional system using the app is managing twelve routes, and the app handles that task better than any product the city would approve.
examples.whatToDo: Assess the regional app against the regional network's requirements before concluding it is weak. The city's minimum requirements are correct for the city's network. They are not the relevant standard for a system running twelve routes.
examples.whyItMatters: Minimum requirements set by a large network reflect what that network needs. An app that fails those minimums may be exactly right for a smaller network operating under different constraints, for the same reasons it fails the large system's evaluation.

examples.title: Sophie's Postmortem Confirms Every Decision Was Right
examples.scenario: It took Sophie's team three months to complete the postmortem on the credit union lending tool, and every finding confirmed the original decision. The loan sizes were below the bank's minimum. The approval criteria were too simple for mid-market commercial underwriting. The documentation trail was too thin. The postmortem confirmed each step, closed the file, and recorded no explanation for why the credit union's small-business portfolio had grown faster than the bank's over the same three-year period.
examples.whatToDo: Include the credit union's growth data in the postmortem analysis and ask which borrower segment drove it. The bank's model produced a correct evaluation of the tool for the bank's network. It produced no analysis of the borrower network the tool actually serves.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem that confirms each decision was correct within the current model can still miss the strategic question of why a different organization, serving a different network with different standards, grew faster over the same period.

examples.title: Kiran's Before-and-After Starts in a Radiology Suite
examples.scenario: The hospital radiology suite has a ceiling-mounted imaging arm and three trained technicians. The portable ultrasound being evaluated is handheld, about the size of a large phone. Before: Kiran runs it against hospital imaging standards. It fails on resolution, reimbursement classification, and regulatory pathway. After: two years into rural clinic deployment, the clinics that adopted it have diagnostic capability they never had before, because they are not substituting for hospital equipment. They are using something that previously did not exist in their setting.
examples.whatToDo: Evaluate the portable unit against the standards of the rural clinic network before closing it out on hospital criteria. The hospital evaluation is correct for the hospital's network. It produces no information about the clinical context where the device is actually deployed.
examples.whyItMatters: A device that falls short of replacing existing capability in one network may represent a genuine capability gain in a network where no comparable tool existed. The two evaluations are not measuring the same thing.

questions.prompt: The company describes its market research process as comprehensive because it surveys all major customer segments. A new product for a segment outside its current network still fails to surface through the process. What does this reveal about the process?
choices: The process may accurately reflect what customers in the current network need while producing no information about whether those requirements apply in a different network.
The process should use a larger sample size and include broader demographic categories to be statistically valid.

The firm's revenue concentration in the major segments makes their requirements the highest-stake feedback signal, so survey frequency should track revenue weight rather than spreading coverage evenly across all account tiers regardless of size.
questions.explanation: Comprehensive coverage of current customer segments accurately maps the current value network. It cannot describe a different network where different performance criteria apply. The gap is structural, not a survey size problem.

questions.prompt: The product team evaluates a simplified simulation tool against the eight precision criteria used by their aerospace customers. The tool passes two criteria. Independent mechanics at regional repair shops use it as their primary instrument. What does this gap reveal?
choices: Whether the development team's capacity to add the six failing features would require design changes that compromise the performance characteristics the mechanics value in the simplified version.
Whether there is a user community where the two criteria the tool passes are the load-bearing ones and the six failing criteria are not relevant.

Whether the simplified tool's price point relative to the flagship creates a market segment where the tool's two passing features are sufficient and the flagship's additional features represent unnecessary overhead.
questions.explanation: The six failing criteria are load-bearing in the aerospace network. They may not apply in a maker or prototype community with different requirements. Shelving the tool without asking this question treats one network's standards as universal.

questions.prompt: The tablet-based checklist app fails a commercial airline's compliance audit because it lacks six required fields. Independent mechanics in regional repair shops use it as their primary documentation tool. What does this outcome most accurately reveal?
choices: The independent mechanics in regional shops are using the app in a context where the six missing fields are not required by their regulatory framework, so the gap reflects regulatory scope rather than a technical deficiency in the app itself.

The audit methodology assigns equal weight to all six missing fields, but in regional maintenance contexts where compliance requirements were written for large carriers, some fields may be structurally inapplicable to the work the mechanics perform.
The compliance requirements were built for the airline network, where those fields are legally mandated, not for the independent mechanic network, where they are not.
questions.explanation: Compliance requirements reflect the standards of the network that generated them. The airline's requirements are correct for the airline's network. The independent mechanic operates under different regulatory conditions where those six fields do not apply. Both assessments can be accurate simultaneously.

questions.prompt: The regional transit app handles twelve routes well but fails the city transit authority's minimum requirements for payment processing and multimodal transfers. What does this mismatch most accurately reveal about the evaluation?
choices: The city's minimum requirements were set for a system managing three hundred routes, not twelve. The app succeeds in the smaller network for the same reasons it fails the larger one.

The technology director's evaluation framework applies requirements written for a 300-route system uniformly, which may be the right standard for citywide deployment but conflates minimum viable performance at 12 routes with minimum viable performance at the scale the city's system requires.

The city's minimum requirements were calibrated to a network managing 300 routes, and applying those thresholds to a 12-route system evaluates compliance infrastructure before scale rather than testing whether the system can serve its actual current user base.
questions.explanation: The city's minimum requirements reflect what three hundred routes demand. An app built for twelve routes is not in the same value network. The app's limitations relative to the city's requirements are precisely what makes it well-matched to the regional network.

questions.prompt: Evaluating a credit union's lending tool, a bank concludes it is below threshold because the loan sizes are too small and documentation is too light. The credit union serves a borrower market the bank does not. What does this evaluation most accurately reveal?
choices: The bank's analysis was correct for the bank's network. The credit union's tool served a borrower network where the bank's underwriting standards are not the relevant ones.

The bank's product team should have evaluated whether the credit union's loan-size distribution reflects a deliberately different borrower profile rather than a gap in underwriting capacity, before using the bank's own minimum loan threshold as the pass-fail criterion.

The bank's underwriting criteria were built from its own borrower data, which skews toward loan sizes and income profiles that may not describe the credit union's market, making the evaluation a comparison of two different borrower populations rather than an assessment of tool quality.
questions.explanation: The bank's underwriting standard is correct for mid-market commercial lending. The credit union's tool serves first-time small-business borrowers whose needs do not map to that standard. The bank's evaluation was accurate for its own network and silent on the other one.

questions.prompt: The product director argues that the company's evaluation process is sound because it applies the same criteria consistently to all products. The evaluation rejects a simplified tool that independent mechanics have adopted as their primary instrument. Which question should be asked?
choices: The criteria should be calibrated once per market segment rather than once per product, so that a simplified tool evaluated for independent-mechanic use faces criteria drawn from that market's actual requirements rather than from the aerospace customer's performance specifications.

Consistent criteria applied to all products will give equally valid results as long as all products are competing to serve the same network, but the argument does not address whether the mechanics' tool is competing to serve the aerospace customer at all.
Criteria that were built from current customer requirements will consistently reject products that fit a different network, even when those products are commercially viable in that network.
questions.explanation: Consistency in applying criteria is a property of the process, not a property of the criteria's coverage. If the criteria were built from one value network, consistent application will consistently favor that network and consistently reject the other.

questions.prompt: A portable ultrasound fails a hospital evaluation on resolution, reimbursement classification, and regulatory pathway. Rural clinics report that the same device gave them diagnostic capability they previously lacked. Which statement best explains why both can be true?
choices: The hospital evaluation is correct for a network where full diagnostic capability is required. The rural clinic assessment reflects a network where any portable diagnostic capability is a gain.

The rural clinics' diagnostic workflow does not require the full documentation depth the hospital's reimbursement process needs, so the three criteria the portable device failed reflect requirements that the rural deployment context structurally does not generate.

The portable device's technical specifications are identical in both deployments, which means the performance gap the hospital identified reflects criteria calibrated to the hospital network's reimbursement requirements rather than the device's absolute capability.
questions.explanation: The hospital is measuring whether the device can substitute for existing diagnostic equipment. The rural clinic is measuring whether the device adds diagnostic capability that did not previously exist in their setting. These are different questions applied in different networks.

questions.prompt: A warehouse distributor evaluates a small-batch consumer product by running it through the unit economics model used for restaurant accounts. The product fails on cost per unit, minimum order, and delivery margin. What does this evaluation reveal and what does it conceal?
choices: It reveals the product fails the unit economics threshold built for restaurant-account volumes and conceals whether the product's cost structure could be viable through a retail channel where volume-per-SKU requirements differ from restaurant replenishment patterns.

It reveals a unit economics gap under the restaurant account model and fails to assess whether the same cost structure could achieve viability in a direct-to-consumer channel where margin requirements and order frequency differ from the distributor's requirements.
It reveals the product fails the restaurant account model accurately and conceals whether a different distribution structure would produce a different result.
questions.explanation: The restaurant account model is the measuring instrument applied here. The model is accurate for restaurant accounts. It cannot show whether the product is viable under a direct-to-consumer distribution model with different margin requirements and different order structures.

questions.prompt: A postmortem confirms that a product acquisition decision was correct by every criterion used in the original evaluation. The product later succeeds at a competitor who serves a different market. What is the most important thing the postmortem should add?
choices: An analysis of whether the competitor's development team identified the market opportunity through criteria the postmortem's framework did not include, which would explain how both teams could apply similar logic and reach different commercial outcomes.
An audit of which evaluation criteria drove the decision and whether those criteria apply in the market where the product succeeded.

A reassessment of whether the criteria the postmortem validated are capable of identifying emerging-market opportunities, given that those criteria correctly predicted the failure and did not predict the competitor's subsequent success.
questions.explanation: A postmortem that confirms the process was correctly applied does not address whether the process was measuring the right things. The competitor's success in a different market is evidence that the evaluation criteria were specific to one network, not universal.

reviewCards.front: Your team just rejected a product because it failed six of eight benchmark criteria. What should you verify before treating that as a final answer?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the six failing criteria apply in the market the product was built for. A benchmark built from current customer requirements confirms your network's standards. It does not confirm whether a different network uses those standards.

reviewCards.front: Why can two companies look at the same product and reach opposite conclusions about its quality?
reviewCards.back: They are applying the standards of different value networks. The same product can fail a network that requires high precision and succeed in one that values lower cost or simpler operation. Both evaluations can be correct.

reviewCards.front: What does a value network include beyond just your customers?
reviewCards.back: Margin requirements, performance standards, planning cycles, distribution structures, and the improvement criteria that determine what gets funded. The whole system shapes what looks worth building.

reviewCards.front: A product serves rural clinics well and fails a hospital evaluation. Is the hospital evaluation wrong?
reviewCards.back: No. The evaluation is correct for the hospital's network. The product operates in a different network where the hospital's requirements do not apply. Both assessments can be accurate at the same time.

reviewCards.front: What happens to a product that fits a different value network when evaluated by your current network's standards?
reviewCards.back: It fails, generates no pull in the resource allocation process, and disappears from the roadmap. The evaluation was correct for your network. The product's actual market was never visible in the evaluation.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to separate which evaluation criteria are specific to your current value network from which are universal, and to apply that distinction before using a rejection to close a file.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new product against current standards
ifThenPlans.plan: If the product fails your quality checklist, then identify which failing criteria are specific to your current network and which would also apply in the market the product was actually built for.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a competitor's product that seems weak
ifThenPlans.plan: If a competitor's tool is gaining share in a market you don't serve, then map which performance criteria matter in that market before concluding the tool is simply inferior to yours.

ifThenPlans.context: making a resource allocation decision about a new product line
ifThenPlans.plan: If the investment case concludes a product is not viable, then verify whether the viability test used your current network's standards or the standards of the market the product was built for.

ifThenPlans.context: running a postmortem on a rejected product that later succeeded elsewhere
ifThenPlans.plan: If the product succeeded in a different market, then audit which evaluation criteria drove the rejection and whether those criteria apply in the network where it succeeded.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one product or technology your organization rejected in the last year. Write down the three criteria that drove the rejection. Then write one sentence about which of those criteria would not apply if a different type of customer used the product.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when evaluating a new product or initiative, write one sentence naming the alternate network where the product might succeed before judging it against your current standards.

memorableLines.text: A value network defines what matters. Your current customers shape that definition, and it becomes your measuring instrument for everything.
That actual market has no vote in your budget meeting.
The frame of the evaluation is too narrow to show you the other network.

chapters.title: Disruptive Technological Change in the Mechanical Excavator Industry
chapters.hook: You do not need to win the mainstream on day one. You need one market where your weaknesses are tolerable.
chapters.counterintuition: A new product that loses to the established leader on every mainstream measure can still be the right move. In fact, winning in the first market requires only that your advantages are real there and your weaknesses do not matter yet.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name the one use case where your product or idea is already the obvious choice. That is your foothold. Write it down before asking whether it can scale.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A disruptive product needs a first market where its weaknesses are tolerable and its advantages are real, then a path toward the mainstream.

breakdown.fastRead:
The cargo bike could not handle pallets, highway routes, or large-volume batches. The freight carrier's evaluation form had four required performance thresholds and the bike failed all of them. The evaluation was honest. The form was also built for the freight carrier's current operations, which meant it was not designed to find the narrow alley beside the coffee shop where a cargo van could not fit.

A disruptive product does not need to win the mainstream test. It needs a first market where the mainstream test does not apply.

Finding that market is the move. Not improving the product until it can beat the incumbent everywhere, but identifying the context where its actual advantages are the ones that matter.
breakdown.deepRead:
Hydraulic excavators entered the market through residential sewage construction, where the backhoe attachment could work in smaller trenches that cable machines could not reach efficiently. Cable machines dominated mainstream earthmoving: payload capacity, reach, and the ability to move large volumes of material in a single pass were what the established market valued. The hydraulic machine was weaker on all of those measures and stronger in a context the mainstream market barely noticed. A hydraulic backhoe digging a residential sewer line was not trying to beat the cable crane at its own work. It was doing a job the cable crane could not do well, in a market the cable crane operator barely noticed.

That foothold was commercially real. It was also invisible to the leaders who were improving their cable machines for the buyers who mattered most to them. The small residential market did not show up on those buyers' purchase orders. It did not appear in their planning process. The hydraulic machine improved there, learned there, and eventually carried those improvements into the markets the cable machines had held.

The pattern is precise. A disruptive product does not defeat the incumbent from the front. It finds a context where the incumbent's performance standards do not govern, establishes a real position there, and follows a trajectory that leads toward the mainstream over time.

This is why an incumbent who acquires or builds the new technology can still arrive late. Owning the technology solves one problem and leaves the harder one untouched. The harder problem is identifying the right first market and allowing the product to be judged by that market's standards rather than the incumbent's. A cable excavator manufacturer who builds a hydraulic machine but tries to sell it to the same earthmoving contractors, on the same performance criteria, has not solved the disruption problem. They have added a product to the wrong network.

The foothold market is not a consolation prize. It is the strategy.
breakdown.fullRead:
Consider what it takes to find the right first market. It is not a matter of lowering your standards or accepting a smaller win. It is a matter of identifying the context where the tradeoffs your product actually offers are the ones the buyer actually needs.

Rachel's cargo bike could carry 80 kilograms. That was enough for the independent coffee roaster on a narrow block in the city center, where delivery trucks idled outside for forty minutes waiting for a loading bay that was always occupied. The freight carrier's evaluation had ruled the bike out in the first five minutes because 80 kilograms was below the carrier's minimum payload threshold. The carrier's threshold was set for the work the carrier did. The coffee roaster's problem was not about payload. It was about the loading bay that was never free.

A product's weaknesses are only weaknesses relative to what the buyer needs to accomplish. In one context, 80 kilograms is too light to matter. In another, it is the whole point, because the vehicle that fits the alley and does not need the loading bay is the only vehicle that gets the delivery made.

The same structure appeared in the excavator transition. The residential sewage contractor was not asking for a machine that could move more earth per hour. The cable machines that dominated large earthmoving were overbuilt for trenching a residential block. What the sewage contractor needed was a machine that could reach a confined space, work without a large crew, and cost less per hour to run. The hydraulic machine's weaknesses on payload and reach were irrelevant in that setting. Its advantages were everything.

This is the foothold question. Not: where can this product eventually compete in the mainstream? But: where are the mainstream product's strengths irrelevant right now, and where does the new product's actual capability solve a real problem?

There is a second part to the lesson that is harder to apply. An incumbent who identifies the right first market and then tries to evaluate the product by the incumbent's own performance standards will still miss the move. Andrew's team built an open-source documentation tool and tried to measure its success against the enterprise knowledge management metrics the company already used: audit trails, access controls, single sign-on integration. The tool failed every metric because it was not built for those metrics. It was built for the kind of collaborative note-taking that six engineers on a product team do in a shared wiki over two days. In that context, the missing enterprise features were not gaps. They were irrelevant. The tool was being measured against the wrong job.

The foothold market requires a different evaluation standard. The product is not trying to win the incumbent's test. It is trying to solve a specific problem in a specific context. Measuring it against the incumbent's full requirement set answers the wrong question.

Owning a new technology is not the same as finding the right first market. That distinction matters because incumbents often acquire or build the disruptive technology and then try to commercialize it through their existing channels, to their existing customers, on their existing performance criteria. The technology is now inside the incumbent. The right first market is still invisible.

examples.title: Rachel's Cargo Bike Fails the Freight Evaluation and Wins the Alley
examples.scenario: The loading dock is twelve meters wide and the freight carrier's evaluation form has four payload thresholds. Rachel's cargo bike fails all four in the first column. The evaluator finishes the table in under five minutes. The bike cannot handle pallets. It cannot run highway routes. It cannot manage the volume batches the carrier's city contracts require. What the evaluation form does not have a row for is the narrow alley two blocks away, where a cargo van sits in traffic for forty minutes waiting for a loading bay that is always full. Rachel must decide whether to accept the evaluation result or ask for a different test.
examples.whatToDo: Find the delivery contexts where the bike's payload limit is not the relevant constraint. The freight carrier's evaluation is accurate for the freight carrier's work. It was not designed to find the problems the bike actually solves.
examples.whyItMatters: A product's weaknesses only matter relative to what the buyer needs to accomplish. A 80-kilogram limit is a disqualifying failure in one context and exactly the right specification in another.

examples.title: Andrew Notices His Team Is Using the Wrong Tool for the Right Reason
examples.scenario: It took Andrew three months to notice that his team had stopped updating the enterprise knowledge management system. They were using a free open-source wiki tool instead, without anyone filing a request or explaining why. The open-source tool has no support SLA, no audit trail, and no SSO integration. IT's checklist flags all three as required. The team is not interested in the checklist. They are interested in the kind of shared page they can edit together in real time during a design session, which the enterprise system handles badly.
examples.whatToDo: Before asking IT to block the tool, identify which specific task the team is using it for. The enterprise system's missing features are gaps in the enterprise system's design context. They are features the open-source tool was never built to have.
examples.whyItMatters: A tool that fails an enterprise compliance checklist may be solving a real problem in a use case the enterprise system was not designed for. The checklist gap is not a flaw. It is evidence of a different job.

examples.title: Lars Evaluates a Route the Major Carrier Left Behind
examples.scenario: At 2:10 p.m. Thursday, Lars opens the discontinued route analysis. The major carrier pulled the service after eighteen months: average load factor at 41 percent, well below the break-even threshold for a 160-seat aircraft. The passenger demand data shows the route exists. It does not show what the break-even load factor is for Lars's 72-seat turboprop. Lars must decide whether to use the major carrier's exit as evidence that the route has no market, or to run the route economics against his own aircraft and cost structure before reaching that conclusion.
examples.whatToDo: Run the route economics against the regional aircraft before accepting the major carrier's exit as a verdict on the route's viability. A route that cannot fill a 160-seat jet may work consistently at 60 percent load on a 72-seat turboprop.
examples.whyItMatters: The major carrier's exit describes what the route could not support for a large aircraft at that carrier's cost structure. It does not describe what the route can support for a smaller aircraft at a different economics baseline.

examples.title: Giulia's Risk Model Flags the Wrong Column
examples.scenario: Which borrower is riskier: a gig delivery driver with no W-2 income, or a salaried employee with a credit score twenty points lower? Giulia's underwriting model scores the delivery driver as high-risk based on income irregularity. The predict: the gig-worker loan product will underperform because the default risk is too high for the standard model. The reveal: a repayment structure tied to weekly platform payouts, rather than monthly salary cycles, produces a default rate within acceptable range because it matches how gig income actually arrives.
examples.whatToDo: Test a repayment structure calibrated to the borrower's actual payment cadence before using the standard risk model to reject the product. The existing model was built for salaried income patterns. Gig income has a different rhythm.
examples.whyItMatters: A risk model built for one income structure will misread risk in a different income structure. The gig worker is not higher risk in general. The model's measure of risk is calibrated to a pattern the borrower does not follow.

examples.title: Ben's Postmortem Nearly Ignores the Small-Firm Data
examples.scenario: The BigLaw pilot postmortem is forty pages. Ben's team documented every gap: multi-jurisdiction analysis, citation validation, brief formatting, precedent cross-referencing, and eight others. The small-firm pilot postmortem is nine pages and nearly was not written at all because the target market was BigLaw. The small-firm practitioners used the tool to review standard commercial contracts and reported that it handled that task faster than anything they had tried. No small firm had asked for multi-jurisdiction analysis. Those twelve capabilities were not on their requirement list.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the small-firm pilot data as a separate finding rather than a footnote to the BigLaw failure. The BigLaw gaps describe what the tool cannot do for the largest firms. They do not describe what it can do for a different class of user.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem written about the wrong pilot will produce accurate findings about the wrong market. The small-firm success was in the data. The team almost filed it under 'not the target' without reading what it said.

examples.title: Devon's Regional Loop Changes the Economics Before and After
examples.scenario: You are reviewing the reusable packaging proposal that Devon evaluated six months ago and rejected. Before: the national chain's supply model requires pickup logistics across forty distribution points, a return network the reusable company does not operate, and a scale of container tracking that its software cannot handle. Cost per unit comes out higher than disposable. After: a regional food distributor, controlling both the outbound delivery and the inbound pickup on a fixed daily loop, has adopted the same system. Their cost per trip is lower than disposable because they never needed the forty-point pickup network. They needed a loop they already ran.
examples.whatToDo: Before applying national supply chain economics to a regional product, identify whether the product's model requires the national infrastructure or only a controlled regional loop. The two use cases are different problems.
examples.whyItMatters: A supply model built for national distribution will find costs that do not exist in a regional loop. The regional operator's advantage is not that the system is better. It is that the system was built for a different scope and the regional loop happens to match it.

questions.prompt: The cargo bike fails a freight carrier's payload, route, and volume thresholds in the first evaluation column. The carrier dismisses it on all three criteria. What does this evaluation tell the carrier, and what does it fail to reveal?
choices: The evaluation is correct for the freight carrier's operations and incorrect as a universal verdict on where the bike can be used commercially.
The freight carrier should have used a different payload threshold because its standard evaluation criteria applied to the wrong competitive context.

The city's recent bike-lane buildout has shifted the cost-per-delivery curve in the cargo bike's favor for the two-mile delivery radius the carrier operates in, making the payload threshold less relevant than infrastructure fit for this specific route profile.
questions.explanation: The carrier's evaluation is accurate for the carrier's work. It says nothing about delivery contexts where payload is not the binding constraint. Using one network's failure as evidence of universal unviability is the error.

questions.prompt: Hydraulic excavators entered the market through residential sewage construction rather than competing with cable machines in large earthmoving. Why was this the right first move?
choices: Cable machines were too expensive for residential contractors to afford, which made hydraulic machines the only cost-viable option for trench work in that segment.
The residential sewage context valued the hydraulic machine's actual advantages and did not depend on the capabilities where cable machines were stronger.
Residential sewage was a larger market than commercial earthmoving at the time.
questions.explanation: The foothold market succeeds because the incumbent's performance standards do not govern it. Residential sewage work required reach into confined spaces, not maximum payload or large-volume throughput. The hydraulic machine's weaknesses were irrelevant there.

questions.prompt: When a major airline discontinued a route after averaging forty-one percent load factor on a 160-seat aircraft, a regional carrier entered with a 40-seat turboprop at seventy-eight percent load factor and comparable revenue per mile. Which question best captures the strategic issue?
choices: Whether the major airline had a better pricing strategy that the regional carrier could have matched to remain competitive on the same route.
Whether the route's passenger demand and the regional aircraft's break-even load factor together produce a viable business at a different economics baseline.
Whether the regional aircraft can eventually be replaced by a larger jet once the route's passenger volume justifies the equipment upgrade investment.
questions.explanation: The major airline's exit describes unviability for one aircraft size and cost structure. A smaller aircraft changes the break-even load factor. The route question must be run against the regional carrier's own economics, not borrowed from the carrier that left.

questions.prompt: The legal tech tool lacks multi-jurisdiction analysis, citation validation, and brief formatting that BigLaw evaluators require. Small criminal defense firms have adopted it for client intake and first-pass research. What is the most important question the evaluation failed to ask?
choices: Small firms have lower quality standards than BigLaw, which explains why the tool performs better there without requiring the additional workflow features.
The small-firm practitioners are using the tool incorrectly by applying it outside its designed use cases and skipping the required workflow steps.
The twelve missing capabilities are required in the BigLaw network and irrelevant in the small-firm network, where different tasks are the daily work.
questions.explanation: The BigLaw requirements reflect the BigLaw work. Standard commercial contract review at a small firm is a different task. The tool's missing capabilities are not gaps for a buyer who does not need them.

questions.prompt: When a company acquires a disruptive technology and tries to sell it to its existing customers using its existing performance metrics, the product fails each evaluation and generates no traction. What does this outcome reveal?
choices: The acquisition solved the technology problem. It left unresolved the question of which first market values the technology's actual advantages and can tolerate its current weaknesses.

The acquisition addressed the technology capability gap but did not resolve the question of which customer population would value the technology's current performance level, leaving the firm without a validated first market before attempting mainstream entry.

The acquisition delivered the new technology into the existing sales process calibrated to the incumbent's customer base, where the acquired technology's performance profile fails on the criteria the incumbent's customers use to evaluate purchases.
questions.explanation: Owning the technology is one step. Finding the right first market is a different step. Selling a disruptive product to current customers through current criteria puts the product in a network where the incumbent's strengths are what matter, which is exactly where the disruptive product loses.

questions.prompt: When a credit union's risk model scores gig delivery drivers as high-risk because their income is irregular, a repayment structure designed around the actual income pattern reveals ninety-four percent on-time performance. What does this reveal about the risk model?
choices: The credit union's risk model was poorly designed by analysts who lacked the expertise to account for income patterns outside the standard employment context.

The firm's actuarial data on gig delivery drivers is thinner than for traditional salaried drivers, so the model is over-extrapolating from small-sample observations that may not reflect the population's repayment behavior as coverage scales.
A risk model calibrated to salaried income patterns will misread risk in a borrower population that follows a different income cadence.
questions.explanation: The model's risk score is a function of how it was built. A model built for monthly salary cycles produces a different result than one built for weekly platform payouts when applied to the same borrower. The model is not wrong; it is calibrated to a different pattern.

questions.prompt: A product team writes a thorough postmortem on a failed BigLaw pilot and a nine-page note on a small-firm pilot that showed strong results. The team files the small-firm note as secondary because BigLaw was the target market. What error does this commit?
choices: The team should have written the postmortem in a different order that foregrounded the small-firm results before analyzing the BigLaw performance data.
The team should have abandoned BigLaw earlier in the development process before committing to the full feature set the enterprise network required.
Filing the successful small-firm result as secondary treats the target market's outcome as the only relevant finding and discards evidence of where the product actually works.
questions.explanation: The right first market may not be the initially targeted market. A successful pilot in a secondary context is evidence of a foothold, not a footnote. Filing it as secondary treats the target market's standards as the only valid measure of the product's viability.

questions.prompt: A national grocery chain evaluates a reusable packaging system and finds it too expensive because of return network complexity and container tracking costs. A regional food distributor on a fixed delivery loop adopts the same system and reports lower cost per trip than disposable. What explains the gap?
choices: The regional distributor negotiated a better price with the packaging company by leveraging its local volume commitments and long-standing supplier relationships.

The firm's existing regional supplier contracts include volume commitments the national alternative cannot match at the negotiated freight rate, making any switch contingent on renegotiating obligations the firm has already made.
The national chain's supply model requires infrastructure the regional loop does not need, producing costs in the national context that do not exist in the regional one.
questions.explanation: The national chain's cost calculation is accurate for a forty-point pickup network. The regional loop runs the same system without that network because the distributor controls both delivery and return. The economics differ because the use cases differ.

questions.prompt: An engineering team evaluates an open-source tool against the enterprise system's audit trail, SSO, and compliance requirements. The tool fails all three. Team members are already using it without permission for shared design sessions. What does the unauthorized use signal?
choices: That the team needs better compliance training to enforce the approved enterprise system and reduce unauthorized tool adoption across departments.
That the enterprise system has a performance gap for a specific type of collaborative work that the open-source tool fills, and that gap is real enough to drive workarounds.
That the open-source tool should be formally adopted as a replacement for the enterprise system.
questions.explanation: Unauthorized workarounds often indicate a real unmet need. The team is not circumventing the enterprise system because they prefer free software. They are circumventing it because it does not handle a specific type of work well. That is foothold evidence.

reviewCards.front: A disruptive product fails the mainstream performance test. Does that mean it has no market?
