reviewCards.back: Not necessarily. The mainstream test is calibrated to mainstream requirements. A different market with different requirements may be exactly where the product's advantages are load-bearing.

reviewCards.front: Why did hydraulic excavators start in residential sewage construction rather than competing directly with cable machines in large earthmoving?
reviewCards.back: Residential sewage required reach in confined spaces, not large payload or volume throughput. The hydraulic machine's weaknesses were irrelevant in that context. Starting there was not a concession. It was the strategy.

reviewCards.front: An incumbent acquires a disruptive technology and tries to sell it to its existing customers. Why might it still arrive late?
reviewCards.back: Owning the technology does not identify the right first market. Selling a disruptive product to current customers through current criteria puts it in a network where the incumbent's performance standards apply, which is where the new product loses.

reviewCards.front: A disruptive product fails the mainstream performance test. How do you identify the right first market for it?
reviewCards.back: Not where the product can eventually compete in the mainstream, but where the incumbent's performance standards are currently irrelevant and the new product's actual advantages solve a real problem.

reviewCards.front: A successful pilot in a secondary market was filed as a footnote to a failed pilot in the target market. What was lost?
reviewCards.back: Evidence of where the product actually works. The right first market may not be the initially targeted market. Treating a secondary success as a footnote discards foothold data.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to identify the first market where your product's specific advantages are the ones that matter, rather than testing it against the mainstream's full requirement set.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a product that fails mainstream performance criteria
ifThenPlans.plan: If the product fails your current performance benchmarks, then identify one specific use case where those benchmarks do not apply and the product's actual advantages solve a real problem.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a pilot that underperformed in the target market
ifThenPlans.plan: If the pilot failed the target market, then check whether secondary users in a different context produced better results before concluding the product has no market.

ifThenPlans.context: acquiring or building a new technology
ifThenPlans.plan: If you have acquired or built a new technology, then identify the first market separately from the technology itself. The right first market may not be your current customer base.

ifThenPlans.context: a competitor exits a market segment as unprofitable
ifThenPlans.plan: If a competitor exits a segment because it doesn't fit their economics, then evaluate whether your own cost structure or scale makes the same segment viable before treating the exit as a verdict on the market.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one product or initiative that failed your organization's performance evaluation. Write down the one use case where the evaluation criteria would not apply and the product's actual advantages would be the relevant ones.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when reviewing a product evaluation or competitive analysis, write one sentence naming the context where the losing product would be the right choice. That context is the foothold to track.

memorableLines.text: A disruptive product does not defeat the incumbent from the front. It finds a context where the incumbent's performance standards do not govern, establishes a real position there, and follows a trajectory that leads toward the mainstream over time.
The foothold market is not a consolation prize. It is the strategy.
The technology is now inside the incumbent. The right first market is still invisible.

chapters.title: What Goes Up, Can't Go Down
chapters.hook: Every market your organization quietly exits becomes the first step of someone else's climb.
chapters.counterintuition: Abandoning a low-margin segment looks like smart financial discipline. It is in fact the moment you hand an entrant their starting position. Unattractive to the incumbent does not mean unimportant to the industry.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one customer segment your organization has stopped actively serving because the margins were thin. Write down what kind of operator could serve them profitably at a smaller scale.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Low-end markets too thin for an incumbent's cost structure can be exactly right for an entrant's. Climbing upmarket creates the gap the entrant fills, one segment at a time.

breakdown.fastRead:
The rebar segment looked like a problem the integrated steel producers were glad to hand off. Low grade, tight margins, heavy volume, minimal differentiation. Every financial measure pointed away from it. The minimills had a different cost structure and a different scale expectation. For them, rebar was commercially real ground. They improved there, learned there, and eventually followed the profitability gradient upward into structural steel and then into higher-value product lines that the integrated producers had once considered secure.

The incumbent's rational retreat created the entrant's entry ramp.

A market can be unattractive to the incumbent and strategically dangerous at the same time. Those two things are not contradictions. They are the same fact described from two different positions.
breakdown.deepRead:
Integrated steel producers moved upmarket because the economics were clear. Higher-value steel products carried better margins, served more sophisticated customers, and produced investment cases that were easy to defend. Rebar, by contrast, was a commodity. Volume-driven, price-sensitive, and dependent on construction cycles that varied unpredictably. A large integrated producer looking at rebar was looking at a segment that consumed capacity without delivering the return that higher-value segments provided. The exit was financially rational.

The steel minimills and the rebar segment make this pattern concrete. Minimills used electric arc furnaces, which let them operate profitably at a fraction of the scale an integrated mill required. Rebar did not look thin at minimill scale. It looked like a business. The minimills entered the rebar segment, competed effectively there, and over time generated the cash and the learning to improve their product quality and reach into adjacent segments. Each time an integrated producer moved upmarket, they vacated another step on the ladder the minimills were climbing.

This is the structure worth seeing. Not that low-end markets are always worth defending. They often are not, at the incumbent's cost structure and scale requirement. The point is that the decision to exit is evaluated against the incumbent's profit logic, not against the logic of an entrant with different economics. A market that is genuinely thin for the incumbent can be genuinely real for a competitor whose numbers are different.

The climb happens one segment at a time. The minimills did not enter structural steel on their first day in the market. They entered rebar, demonstrated that they could compete there, and expanded incrementally. Each segment they entered was one the integrated producers had either left or had started treating as secondary. The foothold built on the segment above it.

Unattractive to us is not the same claim as unattractive in general.
breakdown.fullRead:
Consider how the upmarket migration actually feels from inside the incumbent. Each step looks correct. A business division that moves from commodity steel to specialty steel is reporting better margins, better customers, and cleaner investment cases. The resource allocation meeting approves the move without significant resistance because the case is genuine. The financials improve. The board approves. The firm is becoming leaner, more focused, more profitable per unit of output.

What that sequence cannot show is what is happening below. As the firm climbs, it leaves segments behind. Those segments do not disappear. They become available. An entrant with a different cost structure does not need to win the segments the incumbent values most. They only need to win the segment the incumbent just decided was not worth defending.

Hannah's radio station rationalized the local music exit clearly. National syndication carried higher CPM rates and lower production overhead. The financial case was real. What the case could not show was where the listeners who preferred local music were going. They did not disappear from the market. They became the first reliable audience for a different kind of programming that picked them up after Hannah's station put them down.

The pattern holds across industries and cost structures because the mechanism is simple. Upmarket moves are always easier to justify than downmarket moves. Better margins, clearer customers, stronger investment narratives. Downmarket moves require the opposite: accepting lower margins, serving customers who are harder to profile, building a case that looks smaller than what the current business does. The asymmetry is structural. Incumbents are not making emotional decisions when they climb. They are making the rational decision that their current business model rewards.

What that rational decision produces, reliably, is a gap at the bottom of the market. The gap is real. An entrant with a leaner cost structure, smaller scale requirements, and a different margin expectation can enter that gap and build from it.

You may have a version of this happening in a market you serve. Not necessarily in steel. Maybe in a service tier, a product category, or a customer segment that your current pricing structure treats as unprofitable. The question is not whether the segment is profitable for you. The question is whether it is profitable for a smaller competitor with a different fixed cost base. If it is, the segment is not empty. It is waiting.

The minimill lesson is not that you should defend every low-end segment regardless of economics. It is more specific. Before exiting a segment, ask whether the exit creates a viable starting position for an entrant with different economics. If the answer is yes, the exit is not just a financial decision. It is a strategic one.

examples.title: Diana Drops Local Music and Hands Off Its Audience
examples.scenario: "The CPM on local music is less than half what we get from syndication," the sales director says. Diana has the slot analysis open. Local music costs four times as much per hour to produce as a syndicated talk block and brings in a third of the ad rate. The margin case is clear. National syndication goes in, local music comes out. Diana must decide whether to approve the programming change based on the CPM comparison alone or to ask where the local music listeners will go after the format change.
examples.whatToDo: Track what happens to the local music audience after the slot changes. The CPM analysis is correct for the current programming model. It does not show whether the departed audience becomes someone else's core following.
examples.whyItMatters: Audiences that leave a format because the format was dropped do not disappear from the market. They become the first reliable listeners for whatever picks them up. The CPM analysis cannot measure that transition.

examples.title: Matthew's Portfolio Improves and the Economy Tier Opens Up
examples.scenario: At 11:00 a.m. Monday, Matthew presents the portfolio rationalization results to the board. RevPAR is up fourteen percent. The eight economy properties are under contract or reflagged. The midscale and above segment is performing. Every financial metric the board tracks is moving in the right direction. Matthew must decide whether to recommend accelerating the remaining economy exits or to first map which operators are entering those markets in the properties the chain has vacated.
examples.whatToDo: Map who is entering the economy tier markets the chain has exited before accelerating the next round of property sales. The RevPAR improvement is real. What is not in the report is which competitors are building economies of scale in the markets the chain is leaving.
examples.whyItMatters: A hotel chain that exits economy properties in a market does not eliminate the demand for economy accommodation. An operator with a leaner cost model enters the same market and begins building the local knowledge and scale the chain just gave up.

examples.title: Nicolas Closes Free Access and Does Not Track Where the Readers Go
examples.scenario: The subscriber report shows 94,000 paying readers and a margin structure that makes the paid model clean. The free traffic statistics show 2.1 million monthly visits generating advertising yield that rounds to noise. Nicolas looks at both numbers and closes free access. The paywall goes up on Tuesday morning. The 2.1 million free readers are not in the subscriber database and they do not appear in any subsequent reporting. They are simply no longer in the measurement system.
examples.whatToDo: Track where free readers migrate after the paywall closes. The subscription economics are correct for the subscribers who convert. The readers who leave are not lost prospects. They are an audience that another outlet can now claim.
examples.whyItMatters: Free readers who leave a site after a paywall goes up do not stop reading. They find a different outlet. That outlet has just received a significant audience development it did not have to earn.

examples.title: Paula Stops Taking Rental Listings and Starts Losing Landlords
examples.scenario: Which earns more agent time: a rental listing at two percent commission or a sale at six? Paula's productivity analysis has a clear answer. Rental listings are consuming roughly thirty percent of active agent hours and generating twelve percent of revenue. The prediction: refocusing on sales will improve revenue per agent hour significantly. The reveal: three years later, the landlords who took their rental listings elsewhere are concentrated on a platform that now has their property data, their renewal history, and their contact preferences. The agency does not.
examples.whatToDo: Track where the departing landlords list their properties before closing the rental business unit. The commission analysis is correct for the agency's current model. What is not in the analysis is the customer relationship data the agency is giving away.
examples.whyItMatters: Landlords who move their rental listings to another platform take their property data and relationship history with them. The platform that receives that data knows those landlords better than the agency that served them for years.

examples.title: Mikkel's Postmortem Finds Every Decision Was Right
examples.scenario: The offset presses are running at 91 percent utilization. Mikkel's postmortem on the decision to exit short-run digital printing confirms each step: changeover time per job was three times higher than long-run, equipment margin was 40 percent lower, and floor space allocation favored the offset lines by every measure. The postmortem records no information about the clients who moved their short-run work elsewhere, what those clients are printing now, or how a regional digital print shop nearby has added forty new accounts in the eighteen months since the exit.
examples.whatToDo: Add a section to the postmortem covering where the short-run clients went and what they are printing now. The offset economics are correct. What is not in the analysis is the market position the plant gave up to whoever picked up the short-run work.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem that confirms only the internal economics of an exit cannot show what competitive position the exit created for someone else. Short-run clients who leave go somewhere, and where they go matters for the plant's long-term market position.

examples.title: Chidi's Account Threshold Sends Small Investors Somewhere Else
examples.scenario: You are reviewing the account profitability analysis that Chidi completed before the minimum account size was introduced. Before: accounts below $50,000 cost an average of $420 per year to service and generate $180 in advisory revenue. The math is clear. After: three years later, the discount platform that absorbed those accounts has built profiles on their trading frequency, risk tolerance, tax lot patterns, and account growth rates. Several of those accounts have crossed $50,000. The brokerage is now acquiring them as new customers, without the history the platform has already collected.
examples.whatToDo: Before setting a minimum account size, assess whether the departing accounts carry relationship data or growth trajectories that become more valuable over time. The servicing cost analysis is accurate for today. It cannot show what the accounts look like at $75,000.
examples.whyItMatters: Accounts that leave a brokerage because of a minimum threshold take their history to whoever accepts them. That platform accumulates the behavioral data, loyalty, and eventual account growth that the brokerage declined to keep.

questions.prompt: The large integrated steel producer exits the rebar segment because margins are thin and volume is commodity-grade, and minimills subsequently enter and build share. Which question does the exit decision leave unexamined?
choices: The integrated producer made the exit correctly because rebar is inherently unprofitable.
The minimill took a larger financial risk than the integrated producer because it lacked the capital reserves to absorb a sustained margin loss in a commodity segment.
Rebar is thin for the integrated producer's cost structure and viable for the minimill's. Rationality is relative to the economics of the organization making the decision.
questions.explanation: A segment's attractiveness is not fixed. It is a function of the evaluating firm's cost structure, scale requirements, and margin expectations. The same segment can rationally be exited by one firm and rationally entered by another.

questions.prompt: The hotel chain exits its economy-tier properties to focus on midscale and above, and RevPAR improves significantly. Which question should the board ask before treating the RevPAR improvement as validation of the exit decision?
choices: Whether the economy-tier markets being vacated are being entered by operators with leaner cost structures who will now develop local scale and customer relationships the chain gave up.
Whether the midscale properties are achieving their target occupancy rates after the transition to the new upscale brand affiliation.
Whether the reflagged properties should eventually be reacquired once the economy-tier market demonstrates sufficient revenue recovery to justify the purchase.
questions.explanation: The RevPAR improvement is real and correctly reported. The board presentation describes the upside of the exit without assessing who fills the markets being vacated and what competitive position they build there.

questions.prompt: The brokerage sets a $50,000 minimum account size because accounts below the threshold cost more to service than they generate. What does the minimum-threshold analysis fail to measure?
choices: That the firm's account history shows roughly 40 percent of small accounts that survive the first 24 months reach mid-market scale within five years, making early exit from that segment a real opportunity cost the minimum-threshold analysis should include.
That the analysis measured current revenue accurately but could not show the future account value or the relationship data the departing accounts would take elsewhere.
That the brokerage should have offered lower service costs to keep the small accounts.
questions.explanation: Servicing cost analysis is accurate for current economics. It cannot model account growth trajectories or the behavioral data those accounts carry as they grow. The accounts did not disappear. They grew somewhere else.

questions.prompt: The commercial printing plant exits short-run digital work because changeover time is too high and equipment margins are too thin. Three years later, a digital-only competitor has taken those clients. What is the most important unanswered question?
choices: An analysis of whether the digital print shop entering the short-run segment has a cost structure built around short-run economics rather than offset-converted infrastructure, which would explain a margin profile the incumbent's model cannot match.

A reassessment of whether the clients who departed to the digital print shop are now building a relationship with a supplier whose platform is designed for their order-size pattern rather than adapted from offset operations.
An assessment of where the departing short-run clients went and what competitive position those clients gave the regional shop.
questions.explanation: Confirming that the internal exit economics were correct does not answer the strategic question of what position the exit created for a competitor. The short-run clients went somewhere, and their destination matters.

questions.prompt: When a radio station drops local music programming because CPM rates are half of syndicated content and production costs are higher, a local digital platform captures that audience within eighteen months. What did the CPM-based decision fail to measure?
choices: Whether the local music listeners who depart will become a ready-made audience for a competing format that picks them up.

Whether the syndicated content's CPM advantage is durable in a market where the digital platform capturing the local music audience can sell local advertising against the same demographic the station just vacated.

Whether the local music audience's departure to the digital platform represents a recurring relationship with local content now generating ad revenue for a competitor, or a one-time channel preference the station could recapture.
questions.explanation: The CPM analysis measures the economics of the current programming. It cannot show where the departing audience goes or how much development value that audience represents to whoever receives it.

questions.prompt: A newspaper moves all content behind a paywall and does not track where the 2.1 million free readers go afterward. What is the strategic risk of this omission?
choices: The newspaper cannot report accurate total traffic statistics to advertisers because its audience measurement methodology was built for its print-era reader base.

The newspaper's ad revenue model depends on maintaining a free audience large enough to satisfy advertiser scale requirements, and the 2.1 million readers represent the portion generating impressions the paid subscriber base cannot replace.
A competing outlet that picks up the departing free readers gains a significant audience base that the newspaper built over years but did not capture in the subscriber conversion.
questions.explanation: Free readers who leave after a paywall goes up do not stop reading. They move to an outlet that accepts them. That outlet receives the audience development the newspaper invested in without having to earn it.

questions.prompt: A real estate agency stops taking rental listings because commission rates are too low relative to sales. Three years later, a competing platform holds detailed property and landlord data for the accounts that left. What was the agency's most significant omission?
choices: The agency failed to track whether departing landlords carried relationship data and growth trajectories that had long-term value beyond the immediate transaction.
The agency should have raised its rental commission rates to offset the revenue reduction from departing landlord accounts before exiting the segment.

The trend toward long-term tenancy in the local market is documented across three consecutive years of transaction data, making rental listings the lever with the longer growth tail in the current market cycle rather than in a speculative future one.
questions.explanation: The commission analysis is correct for per-transaction revenue. It cannot capture the value of landlord data accumulated over time or the strategic position built by whoever holds that data as those landlords' portfolios grow.

questions.prompt: Steel minimills entered the rebar segment and then climbed into structural steel and higher-value products over time. Which best describes the mechanism?
choices: Minimills improved their cost structure in one segment and used the cash and learning from that segment to enter adjacent ones as the incumbent exited upward.
Minimills developed superior technology in the rebar segment that transferred directly to higher-value steel.

Minimills applied the cash flow and process learning from rebar operations to fund entry into progressively higher-value segments, using the cost discipline the rebar segment required rather than acquiring the capacity the integrated producers had vacated.
questions.explanation: The foothold strategy works through learning and cash generation in one segment, then expansion into adjacent segments vacated by the incumbent climbing upward. Each integrated producer exit created the next rung on the minimill's ladder.

questions.prompt: A company director argues that exiting a low-margin segment is always the right strategic choice because it improves the firm's overall profitability profile. What is the strongest objection to this reasoning?
choices: Exits decided on quarterly margin metrics in this firm's history have been reversed within 18 months at higher reentry cost than the original margin improvement justified, which makes profitability-driven exit decisions weaker on a full-cycle basis than they appear in the short run.
The exit may improve the firm's profitability while simultaneously creating a viable starting position for an entrant whose economics allow them to serve the segment profitably.

The segment serves as a feeder for the firm's premium tier, and exiting it would forfeit the customer pipeline that has historically converted at a 12 percent rate into higher-margin accounts over a three-year horizon.
questions.explanation: A segment exit can be financially correct for the exiting firm and strategically damaging if it hands an entrant a real starting market. The two facts are not contradictions. They describe the same exit from two different positions.

reviewCards.front: A segment is too thin to defend at your cost structure. Before you exit, what should you check?
reviewCards.back: Check whether an entrant with a leaner cost structure and smaller scale requirements can operate profitably in the same segment. If they can, the exit does not eliminate the segment. It opens it.

reviewCards.front: Why did steel minimills start in the rebar segment rather than competing with integrated producers in high-value steel?
reviewCards.back: Rebar was the segment integrated producers treated as unprofitable. Minimills had a cost structure that made it viable. Starting there gave them cash flow, learning, and a foothold to climb from.

reviewCards.front: A competitor exits a market segment. What strategic question should you ask immediately?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether your economics allow you to enter the segment they vacated profitably. An incumbent's exit often creates the starting position that a different entrant has been waiting for.

reviewCards.front: What makes upmarket migration consistently easier to approve than downmarket moves?
reviewCards.back: Upmarket moves improve margins, bring stronger customers, and produce cleaner investment cases. Downmarket moves do the opposite. The asymmetry is structural, not a failure of imagination.

reviewCards.front: Unattractive to the incumbent. Does that mean unattractive in general?
reviewCards.back: No. A segment that is unattractive at the incumbent's cost structure and scale may be commercially real for an entrant operating at a different scale with a different margin requirement.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to evaluate market exits not only against your own economics but against the economics of an entrant who might find the same segment viable.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a segment exit on profitability grounds
ifThenPlans.plan: If the segment is unprofitable at your cost structure, then identify what cost structure would make it viable and whether an entrant with that structure exists or could enter.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a competitor's exit from a market
ifThenPlans.plan: If a competitor exits a segment your organization serves, then assess whether your economics allow you to serve the customers they are leaving before someone else does.

ifThenPlans.context: improving portfolio metrics by shedding low-margin assets
ifThenPlans.plan: If you are exiting low-margin accounts or properties, then track where those accounts go and what competitive position the recipient builds from them over the following two years.

ifThenPlans.context: setting minimum thresholds for customers, accounts, or orders
ifThenPlans.plan: If a minimum threshold excludes a class of customers, then assess whether those customers carry data, relationship value, or growth trajectories that become more valuable over time.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one customer segment or product category your organization has stopped actively serving in the last three years. Write one sentence about what kind of operator could serve those customers profitably at a different scale.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when reviewing portfolio or market exit decisions, identify one competitor or potential entrant who could enter the vacated segment and map what position they would build there.

memorableLines.text: The incumbent's rational retreat created the entrant's entry ramp.
Unattractive to us is not the same claim as unattractive in general.
Before exiting a segment, ask whether the exit creates a viable starting position for an entrant with different economics.

chapters.title: Managing Disruptive Technological Change
chapters.hook: An evaluation designed for a market that already exists will reliably fail to find value in a market that is still forming.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the care applied to evaluating a disruptive effort, the problem is rarely insufficient rigor. The benchmark the rigor measures against is wrong. A proof demand built for a mature market asks an early effort to supply a kind of evidence that market formation has not yet produced.
chapters.tryThisNow: Think of one new effort in your organization that has been evaluated and found lacking. Write down the two or three criteria it was judged by. Then write one alternative criterion that would measure learning progress rather than mature-market performance.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A disruptive effort in a forming market cannot satisfy mature-market proof demands. Rigor still applies, but aimed at evidence the current stage can actually supply.

breakdown.fastRead:
The resource allocation process that works well for the established business was designed to work well for the established business. It asks for customer evidence, revenue projections, margin expectations, and proof of market size. In a mature market, those requirements are reasonable. They separate good bets from poor ones.

A disruptive effort operates in an immature market. The customers are not yet customers. The revenue model is not yet confirmed. The market size is not yet measurable by any method the standard framework accepts. The effort fails the evaluation, not because the criteria are wrong, but because the market has not yet formed enough to supply what the criteria require.

A proof demand built for a mature market asks an early effort to produce evidence that the market cannot yet supply.
breakdown.deepRead:
Resource allocation systems are built to find and fund the best opportunities the current business knows how to evaluate. The criteria they use, including revenue forecasts, margin projections, customer profiles, and competitive analysis, are appropriate for markets where that data exists and can be reliably observed. Applying them to an early disruptive effort is not bad analysis. It is analysis aimed at a market that does not yet exist in the form the analysis requires. When those criteria meet an immature market, the immature market fails on every dimension the criteria were designed to test.

Failing the wrong standard is not failure.

What an early disruptive effort can supply is different evidence: early-adopter behavior, first-market learning, and iterative progress on the performance attributes the emerging customer base cares about. Those metrics are not inferior. They are appropriate for the stage.

The misapplication is easy to make because mature-market criteria feel like discipline. Applying different criteria to a disruptive effort can feel like lowering the bar. What is actually happening is a redirect, not a reduction. The rigor stays constant. The evidence type changes to match what the market at this stage can supply. That change is not softer. It is more accurate.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think back to the last evaluation meeting where a new effort was presented and found lacking. What criteria were on the scorecard? Revenue projections. Customer acquisition costs. Addressable market size. Margin structure. Competitive differentiation expressed in terms the current business knows how to evaluate. Those criteria are not wrong. They are wrong for an effort at the stage of market formation that early disruptive efforts typically occupy.

The problem does not come from bad intentions. The people running the resource allocation process are applying genuine discipline. They are asking the questions their frameworks teach them to ask. The frameworks were built to allocate resources well across a portfolio of opportunities the organization understands. When a disruptive effort appears in that same allocation process, it is compared to a portfolio it does not resemble yet.

An early disruptive effort in a forming market is not a weaker version of a mature business opportunity. It is a different kind of thing. It can supply evidence about early-adopter behavior, market learning rate, and fit between a product's current weaknesses and a customer's current tolerance for those weaknesses. None of those things convert into the revenue and margin figures the standard framework expects.

The management challenge is separating two questions that feel like one. The first: does this effort pass our standard evaluation? The second: is our standard evaluation the right tool for this effort at this stage? The first question has a clean answer. Most organizations have a practiced response to the first question and no standard process for the second. Answering the second requires knowing what kind of evidence would be appropriate for a market that is still forming.

You can run a different kind of rigor. Instead of a forecast, ask what the early-market evidence shows. Instead of a margin projection, ask what the learning rate has been over the last six months. Instead of customer comparisons to the core business, ask whether there is a customer set for whom the disruptive product's current attributes are genuinely useful, even if those attributes are not the ones the mainstream market will eventually care about. That is not abandoning proof demands. It is calibrating them to what the market can actually supply.

The discipline is not the problem. The benchmark the discipline is aimed at is.

That distinction has a practical implication. Running a disruptive effort through your standard allocation process is not the same as applying no process at all. It is running the wrong process. The right process asks what evidence this market stage can actually supply, and uses that as the criterion for progress. A pilot that shows three months of improving early-adopter engagement is not a weaker signal than a margin projection. It is the strongest signal the stage can produce. Treating it as weaker because it does not convert into numbers the standard framework expects is where the rigor stops being useful.

examples.title: Emily's Scorecard Has Every Mature Criterion Red
examples.scenario: "Does it have Phase II data?" the clinical development director asks. Emily looks at the evaluation scorecard. The spin-out has credible mechanism data, early biomarker signals, and a published scientific team. Every row requiring Phase II results is red. The program is three years from any mid-stage trial. Emily must decide whether to present the findings as a failed evaluation or to propose what criteria would be appropriate for a pre-Phase II asset.
examples.whatToDo: Propose a separate evaluation standard for pre-Phase II assets before the committee votes. The mature scorecard is correct for late-stage acquisitions. Applying it here measures stage, not merit.
examples.whyItMatters: An evaluation scorecard built for mature assets will reliably reject pre-Phase II candidates that lack the data the standard requires. The rejection measures stage, not scientific quality.

examples.title: Daniel's Procurement Standard Flags the Startup as Pending
examples.scenario: The credit ledger shows a pending audit flag beside the startup's entry. The offsets are real: sequestration is documented, satellite imagery confirms coverage, and the methodology is published. The corporate procurement standard requires a full third-party audit, a two-year track record, and minimum credit volume. The startup is eleven months old. Daniel must decide whether to apply the standard as written or to first define what evidence a first-cycle offset provider can actually supply.
examples.whatToDo: Before applying the procurement standard, define what evidence a first-cycle offset provider can supply. The audit requirement fits established suppliers. A new provider cannot satisfy a time-based criterion it has not had time to complete.
examples.whyItMatters: A procurement standard built on multi-year track records will exclude every first-cycle provider regardless of technical quality. The exclusion measures age, not performance.

examples.title: Frida's Board Packet Shows Every Approval Criterion Unmet
examples.scenario: At 9:15 a.m., Frida opens the board packet to the micro-credential review. The pilot shows 87 percent first-semester completion, interest from three employer partners, and a waitlist of forty-two prospective students. The board's approval criteria require multi-year completion rates, an employer adoption survey across ten or more firms, and an accreditation pathway document. The program has one semester of data. Frida must decide whether to table the approval or to define what evidence would be appropriate at this stage.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the mature approval criteria from the question of what evidence is meaningful after one semester. Name what the pilot can supply and propose what would constitute adequate proof for a program at its first semester.
examples.whyItMatters: Approval criteria built for established programs find first-semester data insufficient by definition. That result is accurate for mature programs. It does not show whether the pilot is progressing well for its stage.

examples.title: Tomás Predicts Failure and Closes the Experiment
examples.scenario: What does a newsletter with no revenue and no acquisition cost benchmark tell you about its future value? The editorial pilot has a 54 percent open rate and reader responses consistently naming it the publication they read most carefully. The ROI framework requires a revenue projection and a subscriber acquisition cost before any investment is approved. Both are marked N/A. Tomás predicts the newsletter fails the standard and recommends against expansion. Two years later, the reader segment it was reaching costs three times as much to acquire through paid channels.
examples.whatToDo: Add an engagement quality metric before closing the experiment. The ROI framework fits approved products. It was not designed for early-format discovery, where engagement is the meaningful signal.
examples.whyItMatters: Engagement signals are early evidence of a reader segment's formation. The ROI framework cannot price what it has not yet seen converted. Treating missing acquisition cost data as a disqualifier discards the leading indicator.

examples.title: Grace's Postmortem Confirms Every Gate Was Applied Correctly
examples.scenario: Looking back at the expansion decision that was delayed eighteen months, Grace's postmortem confirms each criterion was correctly applied: twelve farms fell below the statistical threshold, one growing season was too short for multi-season validation, and no certified market size figure existed. The pilot data was promising on every qualitative measure but could not pass any of the three gates. The postmortem does not address what criteria would have been appropriate for a twelve-farm, one-season pilot.
examples.whatToDo: Add a section defining what evidence a one-season pilot can supply and what criteria would distinguish a promising pilot from a weak one at that stage. The commercialization gate is correct for mature products, not pilots.
examples.whyItMatters: Confirming that the commercialization criteria were correctly applied does not answer whether they were the right criteria for a pilot stage. The postmortem needs to close both questions.

examples.title: Aman's Screen Eliminates the Startup Before the Second Column
examples.scenario: The investment screening spreadsheet has the logistics startup highlighted in red at the top of the queue. Before: Aman's investment criteria require steady-state unit economics and a capital efficiency ratio before any Series A commitment. The startup's unit economics are improving but not yet at steady state. It is eliminated in the first screen. After: the criteria are revised to include a six-month unit economics trajectory metric. The same startup passes. The two screens are not equivalent evaluations.
examples.whatToDo: Add a trajectory metric alongside the steady-state requirement before screening early-stage companies. Steady-state economics fit later-stage investments. Progress rate is the meaningful signal at early stage.
examples.whyItMatters: Early-stage companies cannot show steady-state economics at small scale. Requiring it screens based on stage rather than trajectory. A trajectory metric measures what the early stage can actually supply.

questions.prompt: When a disruptive effort fails an organization's standard resource allocation evaluation, what is the most likely explanation for the failure?
choices: The effort was poorly conceived and its target market has been shown to lack sufficient demand to justify further resource allocation.
The evaluation team applied the criteria incorrectly and the process should be rerun with broader committee representation.
The evaluation criteria were designed for mature markets and the disruptive effort operates in an immature one that cannot yet supply the required evidence.
questions.explanation: The standard resource allocation process was built to evaluate the established business. An immature market cannot supply the revenue forecasts, margin benchmarks, and customer data the standard requires. Failing the standard is not evidence of poor merit.

questions.prompt: The pharmaceutical company evaluates a pre-Phase II spin-out using the same scorecard applied to late-stage acquisitions. The spin-out fails the evaluation. What should the investment committee recommend?
choices: Define what evidence a pre-Phase II asset can supply and propose a separate evaluation standard appropriate for that stage.

Approve the spin-out under a conditional structure that requires defined clinical milestones before subsequent tranches release, so that the investment thesis is tested against achievable early-stage evidence rather than mature-stage financial metrics.

Reject the spin-out at this stage but establish the criteria that would qualify it for re-evaluation when Phase II data is available, giving the team a defined path rather than requiring them to guess what threshold the committee would use at the next review.
questions.explanation: The mature scorecard is appropriate for mature assets. A pre-Phase II asset has not yet passed the time-based milestones the standard requires. The correct response is to define what evaluation is appropriate for the stage, not to force the asset through the wrong gate.

questions.prompt: A corporate venture team's criteria require steady-state unit economics before any Series A commitment. An early-stage logistics startup cannot meet this requirement at its current scale. Which addition would make the evaluation stage-appropriate?
choices: Remove the steady-state economics requirement for companies in sectors where market formation typically extends the path to steady-state beyond 18 months, and replace it with a trajectory metric calibrated to the sector's formation period.
Add a unit economics trajectory metric that measures improvement rate over the last six months alongside the steady-state requirement.

Apply the steady-state criterion on a timeline calibrated to the sector's observed formation period rather than using the same twelve-month window for both mature-sector expansions and early-logistics startups building novel networks.
questions.explanation: Adding a trajectory metric does not abandon financial discipline. It redirects the analysis to evidence the early-stage company can actually supply: rate of improvement rather than a steady state it has not yet reached.

questions.prompt: The media company's newsletter pilot has strong open rates and reader engagement but no revenue model and no subscriber acquisition rate above the company's threshold. What should the media company do?
choices: Cancel the newsletter pilot because it has failed the ROI evaluation and the resources should be redirected to established formats.

Approve the newsletter for a second phase designed to test whether the engagement pattern translates into subscriber acquisition at a cost the business model can support, before committing resources at full expansion scale.
Identify what the engagement data reveals about the reader segment's formation and define what evidence would be appropriate for a pilot at this stage.
questions.explanation: Engagement signals are early-stage evidence of market formation. The ROI framework is designed for established formats. Asking what the available data actually shows is not abandoning rigor. It is applying rigor to the evidence the pilot stage can supply.

questions.prompt: A community-college credentialing board has approval criteria requiring multi-year completion rates, an employer survey across ten firms, and an accreditation pathway document. A micro-credential pilot has one semester of data and three employer partners. What is the most stage-appropriate first step?
choices: Define explicitly what evidence would constitute meaningful proof after one semester of a pilot, separate from the evidence required for a fully established program.

Grant provisional approval conditioned on the program delivering a defined completion and placement milestone within one full cohort cycle, using the employer interest as the baseline and the cohort outcome as the qualifying evidence.

Table the evaluation and provide the program with a specific evidence standard achievable within one cohort cycle, rather than applying a two-year completion requirement that assumes market formation the program is still producing.
questions.explanation: The board's standard criteria were built for established programs. A pilot at the end of its first semester cannot supply multi-year data by definition. The stage-appropriate step is to name what kind of evidence is meaningful at this stage, not to apply the mature standard or to simply wait.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between 'Does this effort pass our evaluation standard?' and 'Is our evaluation standard appropriate for this effort?'
choices: They produce equivalent outcomes when the evaluation standard was calibrated to investments in the same market context, because a standard built from relevant evidence will reject efforts that genuinely cannot meet it and correctly pass efforts that can.
The first tests whether the effort meets existing criteria. The second tests whether the criteria are designed for the stage of market development the effort currently occupies.

The second question is relevant when the evaluation standard was calibrated to a different market maturity level than the effort being evaluated — the technology sector is one context where that calibration gap appears, but the issue arises in any sector with an early-market formation dynamic.
questions.explanation: These are distinct questions. An effort can fail a standard that was not designed for its stage without that failure revealing anything about the effort's potential. Conflating the two questions produces resource allocation decisions that are locally rational and strategically wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does applying a mature-market evaluation standard to a disruptive effort feel like discipline rather than a methodological error?
choices: Because the criteria were designed for the organization's current business, where they work well. The same rigor applied to an immature market produces the wrong result for the right-seeming reasons.
Because disruptive efforts are routinely underfunded compared to core business lines, which makes any evaluation standard appear overly demanding regardless of its design.
Because the organization has not yet developed an alternative evaluation standard and defaults to the only framework it currently operates with.
questions.explanation: The mature-market standard is genuinely rigorous for the contexts it was built to evaluate. When applied to an immature market, it produces a confident result that may be technically correct (the effort does not meet the criteria) and strategically misleading, because the criteria were not designed for that stage.

questions.prompt: A sustainability director applies a carbon-offset procurement standard requiring full third-party audit and a two-year track record. A first-cycle startup with credible methodology is rejected. What does the rejection reveal, and what does it fail to reveal?
choices: It reveals that the startup's methodology has not yet been subjected to the third-party review the standard requires after two years of monitoring, and fails to reveal whether the methodology would produce a passing result if evaluated at the stage it has actually reached.

It reveals that the director applied a standard designed for established programs and fails to reveal whether the startup's approach, evaluated against criteria appropriate to its current documentation stage, would qualify for the support the standard was designed to direct.

It reveals that the startup cannot meet time-based criteria it has not had time to complete, and fails to reveal whether the startup's technical quality would pass an appropriately calibrated early-stage evaluation.
questions.explanation: The procurement rejection is accurate within its own logic. The criteria require time the startup has not had. What the rejection cannot reveal is whether the startup would pass a standard designed for first-cycle providers. The methodological question of whether the standard was designed for this stage is left unanswered.

questions.prompt: The VP argues that applying different evaluation standards to disruptive efforts would lower the organization's quality bar. How should this objection be assessed?
choices: The objection is valid: maintaining a single consistent standard across all investments ensures that discipline is applied without category exceptions.
The objection confuses the level of rigor with the type of evidence the rigor is applied to. Stage-appropriate evaluation is not less rigorous. It measures what the market at that stage can supply.

The standard financial criteria were designed for sustaining-innovation evaluation, and applying them to disruptive efforts is a category error that the firm's planning documentation has already acknowledged, making the objection addressable on those same terms.
questions.explanation: The concern about discipline is genuine and worth taking seriously. Stage-appropriate evaluation does not remove rigor. It redirects rigor toward evidence that is meaningful at the current stage of market formation. Precision applied to the wrong evidence type is not more disciplined than precision applied to the right one.

reviewCards.front: A new effort fails your organization's standard evaluation. Before concluding it is not worth pursuing, what question must you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the evaluation criteria were designed for a mature market and whether the effort is operating in a market that is still forming. Failing the standard and failing on merit are not the same result.

reviewCards.front: What kind of evidence can an early-stage disruptive effort supply that a mature-market evaluation framework typically discounts?
reviewCards.back: Early-adopter behavior, first-market learning rate, and fit between the product's current weaknesses and the customer segment's current tolerance for those weaknesses. None of these convert into the revenue and margin figures the standard framework expects.

reviewCards.front: Why is misapplying mature-market criteria to an early disruptive effort not simply a sign of organizational conservatism?
reviewCards.back: Because the criteria were built to evaluate the business the organization knows. Applying them consistently is correct within the established business. The mismatch is structural, not motivational.

reviewCards.front: A resource allocation process rejects a disruptive effort for lacking a credible revenue forecast. What would a stage-appropriate alternative measure instead?
reviewCards.back: Whether the early-market evidence shows learning progress and whether there is a customer set whose current needs the product genuinely serves, even at its current limited performance level.

reviewCards.front: The discipline is not the problem. What is?
reviewCards.back: The benchmark the discipline is aimed at. Rigorous analysis applied to evidence the market cannot yet supply produces a confident result that answers the wrong question.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish the question of whether a disruptive effort passes the standard evaluation from the question of whether the standard evaluation is appropriate for the effort's stage, and to redirect rigor toward evidence the market can actually supply.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a new effort's resource allocation proposal
ifThenPlans.plan: If the effort is operating in a market that is still forming, then identify what evidence the current stage of development can supply and apply a separate evaluation standard calibrated to that evidence before applying the mature-market gate.

ifThenPlans.context: a new initiative fails the standard financial evaluation
ifThenPlans.plan: If the evaluation returns a red result on revenue or margin criteria, then ask whether those criteria require data that an immature market cannot yet supply before treating the result as a final recommendation.

ifThenPlans.context: running a portfolio review that includes early-stage pilots alongside established investments
ifThenPlans.plan: If the portfolio contains both established investments and early-stage pilots, then separate them in the review process and apply stage-appropriate evaluation criteria to each group rather than a single scoring system.

ifThenPlans.context: defending an early-stage initiative to senior leadership
ifThenPlans.plan: If the initiative cannot meet the standard financial criteria, then present the evidence it can supply, including learning rate and early-adopter data, and name explicitly what the mature criteria require and why the market cannot yet produce it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Think of one new effort in your organization that has been evaluated and found lacking. Write down the two or three criteria it was judged by. Then write one alternative criterion that would measure learning progress rather than mature-market performance.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when sitting in a resource allocation meeting, identify one evaluation criterion on the scorecard and ask whether the evidence it requires can be supplied by the market the effort is currently in.

memorableLines.text: A proof demand built for a mature market asks an early effort to produce evidence that the market cannot yet supply.
Failing the wrong standard is not failure.
The discipline is not the problem. The benchmark the discipline is aimed at is.

chapters.title: Give Responsibility for Disruptive Technologies to Organizations Whose Customers Need Them
chapters.hook: The team that owns the new initiative serves customers who do not need it. That is not a leadership problem. It is a placement problem.
chapters.counterintuition: The instinct is to place a disruptive effort where the relevant technical expertise lives. The problem is that technical expertise and customer pull are rarely in the same place. In fact, placement determines whose urgency governs the effort, and urgency follows customers, not capabilities.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A unit prioritizes what its customers reward. Place a disruptive effort where those customers don't pull for it, and it will always lose. Placement determines which customers generate urgency.

breakdown.fastRead:
Organizational units protect what their customers value. A budget meeting inside a corporate banking division is governed by corporate banking customers: their compliance needs, their service expectations, their renewal risks. An initiative that does not serve those customers is an initiative that appears on nobody's urgent list. Strong executive backing does not change this. Executive backing does not generate the daily urgency that customer need generates.

Placing a disruptive effort with the right team is not about finding the best technical home. It is about finding the home whose customers will pull the effort forward. A telemedicine program placed inside the inpatient unit fails not because the technology is wrong or the team is uncommitted, but because inpatients do not need what the technology offers. The right customers are in a different unit.

Placement determines which customers are in the room.
breakdown.deepRead:
Priority-setting in an organizational unit follows customer signals. The customers that generate revenue, require service, and determine renewal decide what work feels urgent. The unit will allocate resources, people, and management attention toward work that those customers reward. Work that those customers do not reward will be deprioritized, scaled back, or absorbed into whatever higher-priority project is running at the time. This is not a failure of will. It is how organizations respond to the incentive environment their customers create. When a disruptive effort lands inside a unit whose customers have no stake in it, the effort is competing against the full weight of that customer environment.

Customer pull is not created by mandate. It is created by placement.

The correction is conceptually simple and organizationally hard. Find the unit whose customers would actually benefit from the disruptive effort. Those customers create the urgency that makes the initiative visible in priority-setting meetings. Without that pull, an initiative can have executive sponsorship, dedicated resources, and clear goals, and still fail to compete for the one thing development requires: consistent, uninterrupted attention.

The most common mistake is treating technical fit as a proxy for customer fit. A product that belongs technically inside the actuarial division may belong organizationally inside the direct-to-consumer team whose customers send weekly behavioral data. The actuarial expertise is an input. The customer pull is the environment the effort needs to survive.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about the last time a new initiative at your organization was prioritized in a resource allocation meeting. What made it urgent? Most of the time urgency comes from a customer. A key account asked for the capability. A segment is threatening to go elsewhere. A partner flagged a delivery risk. The urgency is real and it is generated by a specific customer relationship. Initiatives that are not connected to any of those customer relationships are the ones that get moved to next quarter, then to the quarter after that, until the window that keeps not arriving becomes a quiet cancellation.

This is the placement problem in its most direct form. An initiative housed in a unit whose customers don't generate pull toward it will wait. It will wait for a window in the schedule that arrives only when the customers the unit actually serves have nothing pressing. In practice, customers who fund a unit's legitimacy always have something pressing. The window does not come. What executive backing can do is maintain the initiative on the agenda. What it cannot do is generate the day-to-day urgency that customer need generates.

The organizational logic is simple enough to see once it is named. Each unit serves a customer base. That customer base sets the standard for what matters. An initiative that serves a different customer base brings different needs into the unit, needs that the unit's customers do not share. Those needs feel like overhead rather than priority. They are not treated as overhead because anyone is obstructionist. They are treated as overhead because the customers generating urgency are telling the unit to focus elsewhere.

Julien's streaming studio showed this clearly. The cable programming division's customers were cable operators measuring success by subscriber count and content fill rates. The streaming platform required content measured by engagement duration and platform retention. Those were not metrics any cable operator was asking for. Every editorial decision drifted back toward what cable operators rewarded, because those were the customers whose signals reached the priority-setting process. The streaming studio did not fail to innovate. It responded to the customer environment inside the unit that owned it.

Laura's telemedicine program had the same structure. The inpatient unit held the technical infrastructure. Admitted patients were not candidates for remote follow-up. The urgent-care division down the hall served walk-in patients who preferred not to return in person for routine visits. Those patients never generated a single urgency signal inside the inpatient unit's planning process. The program stalled, not because anyone decided to stall it, but because the customers who could have sustained it were in a different unit.

Finding the right placement means asking a question before asking about technical fit or budget: whose customers would pull toward this effort if it were placed in their unit? That question points to where the initiative belongs. Technical expertise can be transferred. Customer pull cannot be manufactured. The unit whose customers generate pull toward the disruptive effort is the unit that will protect the initiative when priority trade-offs arrive.

An organizational unit will protect what its customers need. If the disruptive effort is not something those customers need, it will be protected by no one.

examples.title: Laura's Telemedicine Kiosk Waits in the Wrong Corridor
examples.scenario: The telemedicine kiosk stands at the end of the inpatient corridor, screen lit and camera mounted, with a sign-in prompt no one has opened. Laura placed the pilot here because the hospital's technical infrastructure and nursing coordination team are in this wing. The inpatient unit's admitted patients are not candidates for remote follow-up. The urgent-care division two floors down sees walk-in patients who would rather not return in person for a ten-minute check-in. No one in that division was part of the placement decision. Eighteen months after launch, the kiosk usage log shows eleven sessions.
examples.whatToDo: Before finalizing placement, identify which patient population the telemedicine format serves and whether those patients are in the inpatient unit. Technical infrastructure can be shared or moved. Customer pull cannot.
examples.whyItMatters: A telemedicine program placed inside a unit whose patients don't need it has no source of customer urgency. Without urgency, the program waits for a priority window that does not open.

examples.title: Ryan's P2P Roadmap Looks Exactly Like Corporate Banking Needs
examples.scenario: Looking back at the mobile P2P product's roadmap, Ryan can trace where each priority came from. Every compliance checkpoint, every API security audit, every institutional transfer specification was a response to a corporate banking customer request. The retail checking customers who would use P2P daily to split bills and transfer small sums are in a different division with a different budget cycle. The retail division was never in the room when the roadmap was approved. The roadmap it produced looks exactly like what corporate banking customers needed and nothing like what retail customers do.
examples.whatToDo: Map roadmap decisions back to which customer base requested them before the next planning cycle. If the retail checking customers who need P2P are not generating roadmap inputs, move the product to the division whose customers will.
examples.whyItMatters: A product roadmap reflects the customers whose signals reach the team building it. If those customers are not the product's target users, the roadmap will serve the wrong customer base regardless of intent.

examples.title: Julien's Brief Arrives Listing Cable Subscribers as the Audience
examples.scenario: At 10:30 a.m., Julien opens the content brief for the streaming studio's first original series. The cable programming division has approved the project. The brief's target audience is listed as cable subscribers, because that is the metric the division's performance review tracks. Julien must decide whether to produce the series for cable engagement metrics, which will satisfy the division's customers, or for streaming platform metrics, which have no advocate in the budget process. The decision is not primarily about content quality. It is about which customer base is in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Before producing streaming-native content, identify whether the streaming platform's audience has representation in the division's priority-setting process. If not, the studio needs a different organizational home.
examples.whyItMatters: A streaming studio inside a cable division will produce content shaped by cable customers because those are the signals that reach the budget process. Organizational placement determines output, not technology.

examples.title: Astrid Predicts Two Years and Gets Two Actuarial Cycles
examples.scenario: Which customers define success in an actuarial division? Underwriters who submit one annual policy review. Astrid's usage-based product needs weekly behavioral data from drivers to function. The actuarial division's cycle was built around the underwriter's annual timeline. The usage-based product is reviewed at the same cadence. Driver feedback is collected once a year. Astrid predicts the product will be market-ready in two years. Two years later, the product's iteration count matches the actuarial review cycle. The driver experience that should have shaped the weekly feedback loop was never in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Before placing the product inside actuarial, identify whether drivers are a customer the division has any process for. Pricing expertise can be accessed without the product living inside actuarial's priority and review cycle.
examples.whyItMatters: A product that needs weekly driver feedback placed inside a division built for annual review cycles will follow the annual cadence. The cadence is not a choice. It is the rhythm the unit's customers require.

examples.title: Luca's Subscription Box Is Curated for the Wrong Customer
examples.scenario: The packing station is set up for bulk wholesale orders, twelve deep and uniform. Beside it, a subscription box sits waiting for curation notes from last Tuesday's wholesale buyer session. Luca's merchandising team knows how to collect wholesale buyer data. Individual subscriber preferences are tracked on a consumer app the team does not access. The subscription box is curated using the data the team knows how to use. Six months in, the boxes reflect wholesale buyer taste, not the preferences of the subscribers receiving them.
examples.whatToDo: Identify where subscriber preference data is held and whether the merchandising team can access it. Curation follows available customer signals. If those signals come from wholesale buyers, the subscription box will serve wholesale buyers.
examples.whyItMatters: A team curates using the customer signals it has access to. If the only accessible signal comes from wholesale buyers, the subscription box serves wholesale buyers. The subscriber's preference is not in the room.

examples.title: Min's On-Demand Jobs Run in the Gaps Between Offset Runs
examples.scenario: You are reviewing the on-demand printing schedule from last month. Every on-demand job ran in the gap between offset press runs. Before: Min's on-demand service is inside the offset plant team whose metric is press utilization. On-demand jobs fill in around offset priority. After: the service moves to the customer accounts team. Customer delivery dates now set the schedule. On-demand jobs run when customers need them, not when the offset presses have space.
examples.whatToDo: Move on-demand scheduling authority to the team whose customers set the delivery dates. Press utilization metrics are correct for the offset team. On-demand scheduling needs to be pulled by a different customer's requirements.
examples.whyItMatters: A schedule governed by press utilization will always fit on-demand jobs around offset priority. Moving scheduling authority to the customer accounts team changes which customer requirements govern the daily plan.

questions.prompt: What determines which work an organizational unit treats as urgent?
choices: The executive strategy that the unit's leadership announces each quarter.
The size of the unit's allocated budget for new initiatives.
The needs of the customers that generate revenue and fund the unit's legitimacy.
questions.explanation: Customer need generates urgency. An organizational unit will protect and prioritize work that its customers reward. Work that those customers do not reward competes against an urgency it cannot match.

questions.prompt: The hospital operations director places a telemedicine pilot inside the inpatient unit because the technical infrastructure is there. The pilot stalls. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Inpatient customers are admitted patients who don't need telemedicine. No customer pull existed inside the unit that owned the effort.

The inpatient unit's technology team had the infrastructure to deploy the system but no clinical case for outpatient connectivity, since the inpatient team's patients are already admitted and the telemedicine platform's value depends on remote access from patients who are not.

The hospital executive team provided the budget the inpatient unit requested, but the inpatient unit's procurement decisions were governed by what its admitted patients needed, which did not include remote consultation tools.
questions.explanation: Placement inside the inpatient unit gave the effort access to technical resources but disconnected it from customers who would use telemedicine. Without customer pull, the effort had no source of urgency inside its host organization.

questions.prompt: The retail bank places its mobile P2P payment product inside the corporate banking division because the compliance team is there. Which outcome is most predictable?
choices: The roadmap will surface both corporate and retail requirements through the review process, but when resources are scarce the product will prioritize the compliance features the corporate banking customers need to continue using the bank's existing services.
The roadmap will be shaped by corporate banking compliance requirements, because those are the customers funding the division's priority-setting.
The roadmap will stall because P2P payment is not technically feasible inside a corporate banking infrastructure.
questions.explanation: A division allocates its roadmap according to the needs of its customers. Corporate banking customers generate compliance requirements. Retail P2P customers generate user experience needs. The division whose customers are corporate banking will produce a compliance-shaped roadmap regardless of intent.

questions.prompt: The streaming studio is housed inside a cable programming division. Cable operators are the division's customers. Streaming subscribers generate no current revenue for the division. Which outcome is most predictable?
choices: The studio will attempt to produce content that works for both audiences, but when the cable operators' renewal cycle aligns with production budget decisions, the content attributes cable operators prioritize will carry more weight in the creative brief.

The studio will produce streaming-native content when the executive team's stated priority holds, but the cable operators' budget influence over the division's resource allocation will create pressure to satisfy cable metrics in content decisions.
The studio will produce content shaped by cable operator metrics because those are the customers whose signals reach the priority-setting process.
questions.explanation: The division's customers are cable operators. Cable operators reward cable performance metrics. The streaming studio lives inside the division's resource allocation and priority-setting system. Over time, customer signals from cable operators will shape the studio's output even if that is not the stated intent.

questions.prompt: A legacy retailer's subscription box pilot is housed inside the merchandising department. Merchandising's customers are wholesale buyers and store planners. Individual subscriber preferences are the signal the subscription box needs. Which result is most likely after two years?
choices: The subscription box will be curated using wholesale buyer feedback because that is the only customer signal the merchandising team knows how to collect and act on.
The subscription box will build a strong individual subscriber data set because the merchandising team is motivated to make it succeed.
The subscription box will develop its own subscriber feedback system independently of the merchandising team's existing processes.
questions.explanation: The merchandising team knows how to collect and respond to wholesale buyer feedback. That is the customer input their processes are built around. An initiative inside that unit will be served by those processes, not by subscriber-level feedback the unit has no system to collect.

questions.prompt: Why does executive backing for a disruptive initiative fail to substitute for customer pull?
choices: Because executives are often not trusted by frontline teams in most organizations, which limits how far their backing can travel below senior leadership.

Because executive backing sets the agenda but does not generate the day-to-day urgency that customer need creates. The priority signals that determine actual resource allocation come from customers, not from executive support.
Because executives lack the technical authority to override a unit's existing priorities and cannot direct resources below the level of their direct reports.
questions.explanation: Executive sponsorship can keep an initiative visible and funded at a nominal level. What it cannot do is generate the persistent urgency that customer need generates daily. Urgency determines what gets consistent attention. Customer pull determines urgency. Placement determines which customers produce that pull.

questions.prompt: A plant manager's on-demand digital printing service is housed inside the offset plant team. The offset team's performance is measured by press utilization and long-run job efficiency. What will happen to on-demand job scheduling over time?
choices: On-demand jobs will be scheduled according to customer delivery dates because that is what the customers need.
On-demand and offset jobs will be scheduled according to a neutral priority system that serves both equally.
On-demand jobs will be scheduled around offset press priority because the metrics that govern the team's performance are offset utilization metrics.
questions.explanation: A team's scheduling decisions follow its performance metrics. If the metrics reward offset utilization, the team will protect offset utilization. On-demand jobs will fill the gaps rather than set the schedule. This is not obstruction. It is the team optimizing for what it is measured on.

questions.prompt: An insurer's usage-based product is housed inside the actuarial division. Actuarial customers are underwriters who work on annual review cycles. The usage-based product requires weekly behavioral data from drivers. What does the actuarial division's review cycle reveal about the product's development pace?
choices: The actuarial review cycle will govern the product's iteration rhythm because the division's processes were built for its customers, not for weekly driver feedback loops.
The usage-based product will force the actuarial division to adopt a weekly iteration cycle because that is what the product requires.

Usage-based pricing in this category depends on real-time telemetry rather than statistical risk pools, so traditional actuarial methods have no direct leverage on the pricing model the usage-based product requires.
questions.explanation: An organizational unit's processes are built for the customers it serves. Actuarial processes are built around annual review cycles because underwriters work on annual timelines. Placing a product that needs weekly driver feedback inside a unit built for annual cycles means the product will follow the actuarial cadence, not create a new one.

questions.prompt: The company argues that customer-fit placement is less important than strong executive commitment because a committed executive can override unit-level resistance. How should this argument be evaluated?
choices: The argument is correct: committed executives with sufficient organizational authority can override any structural constraint if they apply consistent attention and are willing to reassign resources.
