Executive commitment can maintain nominal support for an initiative but cannot replace the day-to-day urgency that comes from serving customers who actually need the effort. Structure generates persistent urgency. Executive commitment does not.
Executive commitment is irrelevant: only organizational structure and resource allocation authority determine what gets prioritized over time.
questions.explanation: Executive support matters but is not sufficient. An executive can keep an initiative alive, funded, and on the agenda. What generates the consistent priority that development requires is customer pull: the daily signal from customers who need what the initiative offers. Without that signal, the effort competes for attention that customer-serving work will always need more urgently.

reviewCards.front: A new initiative keeps losing priority in resource allocation despite executive support. What structural explanation should you investigate first?
reviewCards.back: Investigate whether the team that owns the initiative serves customers who actually need what it offers. If those customers don't generate pull toward the initiative, executive support cannot substitute for the urgency customer need creates.

reviewCards.front: What does 'customer pull' mean in the context of organizational placement?
reviewCards.back: Customer pull is the urgency generated when an organizational unit's customers need what an initiative offers. Initiatives with customer pull inside their host unit are protected and prioritized. Initiatives without it compete against work that customers are actively rewarding.

reviewCards.front: An initiative is placed inside a unit with strong technical expertise but the wrong customers. What happens over time?
reviewCards.back: The initiative's roadmap, scheduling, and priority-setting drift toward the needs of the unit's actual customers. Technical fit cannot substitute for customer fit. Placement determines which customers generate urgency.

reviewCards.front: You are choosing between two teams to own a disruptive initiative. One has technical expertise; the other's customers would actively pull toward it. Which placement factor matters most?
reviewCards.back: Whose customers would pull toward this initiative if it were placed in their unit? Not: which team has the most relevant technical expertise. Customer pull must come from within the host organization's customer base.

reviewCards.front: Why does an initiative's priority-setting problem look like a leadership problem rather than a placement problem?
reviewCards.back: Because the individual decisions that deprioritize the initiative are defensible on their own terms. Each scheduling conflict or budget revision is local. The cumulative effect of wrong placement shows up slowly, as a pattern.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to diagnose whether an initiative is placed inside a unit whose customers generate pull toward it, and to distinguish customer-fit placement from technical-fit placement when choosing where a disruptive effort belongs.

ifThenPlans.context: a new initiative is repeatedly deprioritized despite executive backing
ifThenPlans.plan: If the initiative keeps losing in resource allocation, then identify whose customers are generating urgency inside the owning unit and whether those customers have any need for what the initiative offers. The problem may be placement, not commitment.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding where to house a new disruptive initiative
ifThenPlans.plan: If you are choosing which team owns the initiative, then map each candidate team's three most important customers and ask which of those customer sets would generate pull toward the initiative before considering technical expertise.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a disruptive initiative's roadmap and finding it shaped by the wrong requirements
ifThenPlans.plan: If the roadmap reflects the host unit's customers rather than the initiative's target customers, then treat the roadmap drift as a placement signal: the initiative is inside the wrong organizational home.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating whether an initiative needs a separate team or can stay inside an existing unit
ifThenPlans.plan: If the initiative's target customers differ significantly from the owning unit's current customers, then assess whether those target customers can generate urgency inside the existing unit or whether separation is needed to give the initiative a customer base of its own.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when sitting in a priority-setting or resource allocation meeting, identify which customer sent the signal that made one initiative urgent and which initiatives lost priority because no customer was pulling for them.

memorableLines.text: Placement determines which customers are in the room.
Customer pull is not created by mandate. It is created by placement.
An organizational unit will protect what its customers need. If the disruptive effort is not something those customers need, it will be protected by no one.

chapters.title: Match the Size of the Organization to the Size of the Market
chapters.hook: Your growth threshold is not a property of the market. It is a property of your organization.
chapters.counterintuition: The problem with size filters is not that large organizations apply them. They need to apply them. The problem is treating the filter's output as a verdict on the market itself. A $10 million opportunity rejected because it doesn't move the needle is in fact still a $10 million opportunity. Someone with different economics will find it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Think of one market opportunity your organization has evaluated and passed on because the size was too small. Write down the revenue or impact threshold that ruled it out. Then write one sentence describing what size of organization would find that exact number meaningful.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Growth thresholds measure fit with your current scale, not the market's absolute viability. A market too small for one organization can be genuinely real for a smaller team.

breakdown.fastRead:
Large organizations evaluate market opportunities against thresholds that make their growth logic work. A market that adds less than two percent to revenue is a distraction at the current scale, even if the underlying opportunity is real. The threshold is not wrong. It is calibrated to the organization that applies it, and it performs exactly as designed.

The error is not in applying the threshold. The error is treating the threshold's output as a verdict on the opportunity rather than a verdict on the fit between the opportunity and the organization's current size. A market that is too small to move a large unit's numbers can be commercially real for a team with different economics and a lower floor for what counts as meaningful.

The filter is calibrated to your organization, not to the opportunity.
breakdown.deepRead:
Growth thresholds are built from the inside out. They reflect what the organization needs a market to contribute to make investment worth the operational overhead. A unit that requires thirty percent annual volume growth to satisfy its board has a real reason to require that from every opportunity it evaluates. Applying a lower standard to emerging markets would mean accepting opportunities that distract from the performance goals the organization actually needs to meet. The threshold is doing exactly what it was designed to do. The problem is not the threshold. The problem is treating the threshold's output as a verdict on the market rather than a verdict on the fit between the market and the organization's current scale.

Too small for us is not the same claim as too small.

An emerging market that generates $8 million in year three looks negligible against a $50 million pipeline threshold. The same $8 million is a real business to an operator whose overhead is different and whose growth requirement is calibrated to a smaller base. The market did not change between those two evaluations. The lens did.

This is the relative materiality problem. Market size is not an absolute number. It is a ratio between the opportunity's size and the evaluating organization's requirements. A large organization applying its own ratio to every market it sees will correctly identify many markets as too small for it. That list is not a list of markets that are too small. It is a list of markets that are too small for that organization at its current scale.
breakdown.fullRead:
What is your organization's growth threshold? Not the aspiration: the floor. The number a market opportunity has to clear before it earns a resource allocation discussion. Most organizations have one, even when it is not written down. It shows up in conversations about minimum viable deal size, minimum addressable market, minimum return on investment. The threshold is real and it functions as a filter. It keeps the organization focused on opportunities that can actually move its economics. It also keeps the organization blind to opportunities that cannot.

Now think about what that threshold makes invisible. Any market that clears a smaller competitor's threshold but not yours. Any opportunity that would be meaningful to a team operating at a lower cost base. Any emerging market that is commercially real but not yet large enough to matter at your organization's scale. Your growth threshold filters all of those out. It does so accurately, from your organization's perspective. From a different position, those markets look different.

The management challenge is knowing when to trust the filter and when to suspect it. Trusting the filter is appropriate when you are allocating your current organization's resources to markets that will actually move your current performance. Suspecting the filter is appropriate when you are making a judgment about whether a market matters at all, rather than whether it matters to you at your current size. Those are different questions, and the threshold is designed to answer only one of them.

Megan's IoT platform review illustrates the second case. The $8 million year-three projection was correctly rejected by the innovation lab's $50 million pipeline threshold. The lab was right that $8 million would not move the corporate needle. What the lab's filter could not show was whether $8 million was a real number in an absolute sense. It was. A building maintenance cooperative found the same number meaningful and licensed the technology. The market did not fail. The threshold generated the wrong question: not 'is this a real market?' but 'does this market meet our bar?'

Jonas's postmortem found the dental SaaS decision correct inside the consultancy's billing model. $180,000 in annual recurring revenue cannot justify partner attention at $800,000 per engagement. The decision was locally rational. The three-person team that built the same product without that billing overhead found the same $180,000 a real starting point. The consultancy did not fail to see the opportunity. It evaluated it correctly against its own scale.

Your growth threshold is not a verdict on the opportunity. It is a verdict on the fit between the opportunity and your organization's current size.

examples.title: Megan's Pipeline Review Flags the IoT Platform at the Bottom
examples.scenario: "Does it hit fifty million in year three?" someone at the back of the room asks. Megan looks at the projection. Year three revenue for the IoT platform across the twelve pilot buildings: $8 million. The innovation lab's pipeline threshold is $50 million. The sensor data is credible, the building performance results are real, and the maintenance cost reduction is documented. The $8 million estimate is also real. Megan must decide whether to present the full technical case or to note the threshold gap and recommend moving on.
examples.whatToDo: Present the technical case and the $8 million projection separately from the pipeline threshold verdict. The threshold correctly filters by lab economics. It should not be the only conclusion recorded about the market.
examples.whyItMatters: A market rejected at the $50 million gate has not been shown to be commercially non-viable. It is a market that does not meet one organization's scale requirement. Those are different findings.

examples.title: Jack's Distribution Model Shows 4 Percent and the Board Moves On
examples.scenario: The seasonal specialty run is a single batch cooling in the tank beside eight lager rows. Jack's distribution model shows the specialty line adding 4% volume nationally at full distribution. The board's growth requirement is 30% per year. The 4% figure reflects real sellout data from the regional market and it is not going to move the number the board tracks. Jack must decide whether to propose the national pilot or to acknowledge that the 4% does not satisfy the investment threshold and recommend focusing on the core lager lines.
examples.whatToDo: Present the 4% projection alongside a note on what kind of operation would find that number meaningful before closing the evaluation. The board's threshold is correct for the brewery's economics. It is not a verdict on the market.
examples.whyItMatters: A 4% volume addition that the brewery correctly rejects can represent an entire product line for a smaller operation. The rejection reveals scale fit, not market viability.

examples.title: Antoine's Market Size Chart Puts Veterinary at 2.5 Percent
examples.scenario: At 2:00 p.m., Antoine reviews the veterinary market entry analysis. Total addressable market for the imaging technology in veterinary clinics: $12 million annually. The company's hospital radiology deals close at $200,000 each. Redeploying the sales force from hospital deals to veterinary clinics would cost more than the market returns at the company's current cost structure. Antoine logs the analysis as a pass on the veterinary channel. The report reads: too small for the current sales model. A veterinary equipment distributor for whom $12 million is a significant line is reading the same number differently.
examples.whatToDo: Document the $12 million market finding separately from the verdict that the current sales model cannot serve it efficiently. A veterinary distributor operating at lower cost may enter the market the company declines.
examples.whyItMatters: A market the company's sales force cannot serve profitably is still a real market. A distributor with lower overhead and a different scale requirement can enter and serve it. The company's rejection does not clear the market.

examples.title: Chiara Predicts the Slate Fails Threshold and Recommends Passing
examples.scenario: Can arthouse titles averaging $600,000 in domestic theatrical justify a distribution investment at a studio with a $2 million per-title minimum? Chiara's evaluation gives the same answer each time: no. The films are critically regarded, the audience is identifiable, and the numbers are still below threshold. Chiara predicts the slate fails the minimum and recommends passing. Two years later, a boutique distributor acquires the same slate, builds a theatrical-and-streaming hybrid release, and the audience becomes a subscriber base the studio later pays to reach.
examples.whatToDo: Record what kind of distributor would find $600,000 per title viable before closing the evaluation. The studio's minimum is correct for its overhead. It is not a statement about the audience's value to someone with different economics.
examples.whyItMatters: An audience the studio passed on for scale reasons does not disappear from the market. A boutique distributor with lower overhead acquires it. The studio's threshold correctly measured fit for its economics, not for the market.

examples.title: Jonas's Postmortem Confirms the Decision Was Correct Inside the Billing Model
examples.scenario: Looking back at the dental SaaS decision, Jonas's postmortem confirms the logic: $180,000 in annual recurring revenue cannot justify partner time at $800,000 per engagement. The calculation was sound. The postmortem also notes that a three-person team, operating without billing-hour overhead, built the same product and now manages 400 dental offices. The decision log reads: 'insufficient return for partner time.' It does not address what the same number looked like to a team with different economics.
examples.whatToDo: Add a line to the decision log describing the cost structure that would make $180,000 ARR viable. The consultancy's rejection was correct for its own model. It should not be recorded as a verdict on the market.
examples.whyItMatters: A revenue figure that cannot justify partner time at one firm can be the starting point for a team operating at a fraction of that overhead. Recording only the internal verdict loses the distinction between scale fit and market viability.

examples.title: Hadiya's Site Plan Shows 14 Units Beside an 80-Unit Annual Goal
examples.scenario: The meeting room projector shows a site plan: fourteen small structures on an undeveloped lot. On the right side is the land trust's annual goal: eighty permanently affordable units. Hadiya presents the tiny-home pilot. The board's resource allocation process is built around projects that contribute meaningfully to the eighty-unit goal. Fourteen does not. Before: the board defers the pilot. After: a separate community land trust, using the same model, scales from fourteen units to one hundred forty across four pilots.
examples.whatToDo: Record the board's threshold separately from any conclusion about the model's scale potential. The 14-unit pilot does not meet the 80-unit annual requirement. That is not the same finding as the model cannot scale.
examples.whyItMatters: A pilot size that does not meet one organization's annual threshold can be the starting point for a different organization with different resource constraints. The threshold belongs to the land trust, not to the model.

questions.prompt: The large organization evaluates a $10 million market opportunity and rejects it because it does not clear the growth threshold. What does the threshold reveal, and what does it conceal?
choices: The market's commercial viability should be assessed against the cost structure and minimum return requirements of the organization evaluating it rather than treated as an inherent property of the market that applies to all potential entrants.

The market's revenue potential is too small relative to the evaluating organization's overhead and margin requirements to justify the sales team, management attention, and support infrastructure the entry would require.
The market does not meet the evaluating organization's threshold. That reveals something about scale fit, not about the market's viability in absolute terms.
questions.explanation: A growth threshold is calibrated to the organization that applies it. Failing the threshold reveals a mismatch between the opportunity's size and the organization's requirements. It does not tell you whether the opportunity is real for a differently sized organization.

questions.prompt: The craft brewery's board applies a 30 percent annual volume growth requirement to all investments. The seasonal specialty line adds 12 percent annually and the board rejects it. What is the most important strategic question the threshold fails to answer?
choices: The 4% is too small for the brewery's economics and potentially meaningful for the smaller operation's different economics. Both evaluations are correct relative to their own scale.
The brewery's board made a strategic error by applying a 30% annual volume threshold too rigidly to a specialty product with a different growth profile.
The smaller operation is taking an unacceptable risk by pursuing a market the larger brewery rejected.
questions.explanation: The same market can be too small for one organization's growth threshold and genuinely meaningful for another organization operating at a smaller scale. Both assessments are accurate within their own frame of reference.

questions.prompt: A medical device company's VP evaluates the veterinary market for its imaging technology. The market totals $12M annually. The company's sales force costs more to redeploy than $12M would return. The VP passes. Which outcome is most likely for the veterinary market?
choices: The veterinary market will remain untapped by operators whose overhead and minimum return requirements make $12M insufficient, and will attract entry only from an operator whose cost structure treats $12M as a meaningful return relative to its fixed base.
A veterinary equipment distributor for whom $12M is a significant line will enter the market that the device company passed on.

The device company will re-enter the veterinary market when it grows to a size that justifies the sales infrastructure and regulatory investment its current operating model requires for new segment entry.
questions.explanation: A market rejected by a large organization for scale reasons does not disappear. An entrant with lower overhead and a lower floor for what counts as meaningful can find the same market attractive and enter it.

questions.prompt: A mid-size film studio applies a $2M domestic theatrical minimum per title. An arthouse slate peaks at $600K. The studio passes. A boutique distributor acquires the same slate. What explains why the boutique distributor can find the slate viable?
choices: The boutique distributor's business model is built around arthouse titles with $500K-$800K theatrical potential, so the $600K ceiling the studio rejected represents a target-range result for the boutique rather than a below-threshold outcome.

The boutique distributor's existing arthouse theater network lowers the distribution cost per title, allowing it to profit at a domestic theatrical return that the mid-size studio's overhead structure cannot reach at break-even.
The boutique distributor's overhead is lower, so $600K represents a meaningful return relative to its own cost structure and growth requirements.
questions.explanation: The same title that cannot clear a mid-size studio's minimum is potentially viable for a boutique distributor with lower overhead. The opportunity did not change. The organizational scale evaluating it did.

questions.prompt: The land trust's board passes on a 14-unit tiny-home pilot because it does not meet the 80-unit annual impact threshold. Six months later, the municipality funds a competing pilot. What does this sequence reveal?
choices: The board made a strategic error by not pursuing the tiny-home model itself and should have allocated a small-scale development budget to test the model separately.

The board correctly applied its own threshold but incorrectly treated the threshold's verdict as evidence that the model could not scale, rather than evidence that 14 units did not meet their specific requirement.
The 14-unit threshold is universally too low for any land trust to consider worth pursuing, regardless of the model's potential for replication at other sites.
questions.explanation: The board's rejection was locally correct: 14 units does not meet an 80-unit annual goal. The error would be concluding from that rejection that the model itself has no scale potential. A different organization demonstrated that it does.

questions.prompt: Why do large organizations repeatedly pass on emerging markets that later become meaningful, even when they have thorough evaluation processes?
choices: Because their evaluation processes are designed to match opportunities to their current scale requirements, which emerging markets cannot yet meet. The process is correctly excluding what it was built to exclude.
Because their evaluation processes are poorly designed and do not reliably identify real market opportunities that fall outside their primary revenue categories.

Because the signals that emerging markets produce in their early stages are too diffuse for evaluation processes built around historical revenue patterns to convert into clear entry recommendations before competitors with different thresholds have moved.
questions.explanation: A large organization's evaluation process is designed to find markets that match its current economics. Emerging markets are, by definition, too small to match those economics at first. The process is not broken. It is correctly filtering out markets that are too small for its scale, which is exactly what it was designed to do.

questions.prompt: The software consultancy's partners group rejects a $180K ARR dental SaaS product because their average engagement is $800K. Three months later, a boutique consultancy takes the contract and uses it to build a dental vertical. What is the most important question the partners group failed to ask?
choices: The consultancy's billing overhead made the $180K genuinely unviable for them. The three-person team's lower overhead made the same $180K a real starting point. Both assessments were correct for their respective cost structures.
The consultancy missed a substantial opportunity that its existing technical capabilities would have allowed it to pursue, if it had been willing to develop a lower-overhead delivery structure.
The consultancy's billing model was poorly designed for the software market and reflects an outdated approach to pricing professional services.
questions.explanation: The consultancy correctly evaluated $180K ARR as insufficient to justify partner time at $800K per engagement. The three-person team's economics were different. The same number the consultancy correctly rejected as too small was the right starting point for a team with different overhead.

questions.prompt: A corporate innovation lab's $50M pipeline threshold correctly filters out an $8M IoT platform. A building maintenance cooperative later licenses the same technology and finds $8M meaningful. What is the diagnostic significance of this outcome for the innovation lab's process?
choices: The innovation lab's pipeline threshold is set too high and should be revised downward to expand the range of opportunities it considers.

The innovation lab should have partnered with the cooperative to pursue the opportunity jointly, because the lab's $50M threshold was the right filter for solo entry but should not have prevented a structure where the cooperative's lower overhead absorbed the entry cost.
The innovation lab's threshold correctly measured fit for the lab's scale. The cooperative's entry reveals that the threshold was filtering by organizational fit, not by market viability.
questions.explanation: The innovation lab's filter did its job: $8M is not a meaningful number for a unit requiring $50M. The cooperative's entry reveals that the filter was measuring something specific to the lab's scale requirements. The market was real. The filter was scale-specific. Conflating the two would have produced a wrong conclusion about the market.

questions.prompt: The strategy director argues that if an opportunity is too small for the organization's current threshold, it should not be pursued, and that thresholds represent rigorous market discipline. How should this argument be evaluated?
choices: The position is correct: if an opportunity cannot meet the organization's current threshold, it should not receive organizational attention in any form, including through subsidiaries, spin-outs, or partner relationships.

The position conflates 'too small for the current unit's economics' with 'too small to matter.' A smaller team, subsidiary, or partner with different economics may find the same market genuinely viable, and passing on it entirely means ceding the market to an external entrant.
The position is incorrect: every organization should pursue every market regardless of size in order to maintain market presence and prevent external entrants from establishing footholds.
questions.explanation: A growth threshold measures fit with the current organization's scale. It does not reveal whether the market is worth pursuing by a differently structured entity. Applying the same threshold to a subsidiary or spin-out ignores that the threshold is calibrated to the parent's economics, not to the subsidiary's.

reviewCards.front: An emerging market does not meet your organization's growth threshold. Before passing, what question should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the threshold reflects your organization's scale requirements or whether it reveals something absolute about the market. If the market is real but too small for your current economics, a differently sized team may find it meaningful.

reviewCards.front: What does relative materiality mean in the context of market size evaluation?
reviewCards.back: Relative materiality means that the same market can be too small to matter to a large organization and genuinely significant to a smaller team with lower overhead and lower growth requirements. Market viability is always relative to the evaluating organization's scale.

reviewCards.front: A competitor with lower overhead enters a market your organization passed on for being too small. What does this reveal about the original rejection?
reviewCards.back: It reveals that the rejection correctly measured scale fit but may have incorrectly treated scale fit as a verdict on the market. The competitor's entry shows the market was real. Your threshold was calibrated to your organization, not to the market.

reviewCards.front: An emerging market fails your organization's growth threshold. A smaller competitor enters it profitably. What is being confused when the threshold is treated as a verdict on the market itself?
reviewCards.back: 'Too small for us' is a comparison between the opportunity's size and your organization's scale requirements. 'Too small' would be a universal claim about the market itself. The first is usually supportable. The second requires a different kind of evidence.

reviewCards.front: Why must growth thresholds be applied carefully when evaluating emerging markets?
reviewCards.back: Because emerging markets start small by definition. A threshold calibrated to the current organization's mature-market economics will correctly reject many emerging markets as too small at their current stage, even if they would become significant over time.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish between 'this market is too small for our organization's economics' and 'this market is too small to be commercially viable,' and to apply size evaluations relative to organizational scale rather than as absolute verdicts on the market.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating an emerging market against the organization's growth threshold
ifThenPlans.plan: If the market fails the threshold, then explicitly record whether the verdict reflects a scale mismatch or a genuine market problem. Those are different findings and should be documented as such.

ifThenPlans.context: recommending that an organization pass on a market for being too small
ifThenPlans.plan: If the recommendation is to pass, then name the size of organization that would find the market meaningful and assess whether passing cedes a market position to a potential entrant with different economics.

ifThenPlans.context: a smaller subsidiary or partner is considering entering a market the parent passed on
ifThenPlans.plan: If the subsidiary or partner has lower overhead and lower growth requirements, then evaluate the market against their scale, not the parent's threshold. The market may be viable at one scale and not viable at another.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing past rejections of markets that have since grown
ifThenPlans.plan: If a market your organization passed on has grown and an entrant is now established there, then identify what the entrant's economics were at entry. The market's growth does not mean the original rejection was wrong. It means the entrant had a scale fit your organization did not.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Think of one market opportunity your organization has evaluated and passed on because the size was too small. Write down the revenue or impact threshold that ruled it out. Then write one sentence describing what size of organization would find that exact number meaningful.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when a market or opportunity is rejected for being too small, write one sentence about what size of organization would find the same number meaningful. Over time, this builds a habit of separating scale-fit verdicts from market-viability verdicts.

memorableLines.text: The filter is calibrated to your organization, not to the opportunity.
Too small for us is not the same claim as too small.
Your growth threshold is not a verdict on the opportunity. It is a verdict on the fit between the opportunity and your organization's current size.

chapters.title: Discovering New and Emerging Markets
chapters.hook: Forecasting an emerging market before entering it is asking a model to answer a question only real contact can answer.
chapters.counterintuition: Demanding a clean forecast before entering an emerging market feels like sound discipline. In fact, it is a way of requiring that the market explain itself before you can learn anything from it. Emerging markets cannot produce a forecast. That is what makes them emerging. Discovery is what happens between not-knowing and knowing, and it requires contact, not a model.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one market your organization has decided it cannot enter yet because the forecast isn't clear enough. Write down one specific question, not a forecast but a concrete question, that real contact with potential users would let you answer within the next month.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Emerging markets lack the information forecasts require. The discipline is to enter with clear learning questions and organized contact. Discovery produces information that forecasts cannot.

breakdown.fastRead:
Emerging markets are underdefined at the start. The first users are not confirmed. The use contexts are not mapped. The demand patterns are not measurable by any model the organization has built, because no one has yet created the observations those models require. Demanding a forecast before entering is demanding that the market explain itself before the organization will listen.

The first stage of entry in an emerging market is not a forecasting exercise. It is a contact exercise. The team goes in with questions rather than projections: specific questions about use, adoption barriers, and the gap between what the product offers and what real users need. The answers arrive from contact, not from modeling.

A model built on what you know cannot tell you what first users will teach you.
breakdown.deepRead:
Forecast-first thinking assumes that the relevant information about a market already exists somewhere and that enough analysis can locate it. In a mature market, that assumption is often reasonable. The customers are known. The purchase drivers have been studied. The competitive position is documented. Forecasting in a mature market is an exercise in organizing existing information into a probability estimate.

In an emerging market, the relevant information does not yet exist in organized form. Who the first adopters will be, how they will use the product, which performance dimensions they actually care about, and what would make them recommend it to others: none of those things are knowable from a distance. They are knowable from contact. The information that can distinguish a real opportunity from a false one in an emerging market is information that real use generates.

Discovery is disciplined. The discipline is aimed at learning, not forecasting.

Disciplined discovery is organized around what the team needs to find out. It is not general inquiry. It knows what questions it is trying to answer, what kinds of use will count as relevant evidence, and what conditions would change the team's current view of the opportunity. That structure is what separates disciplined discovery from wandering. The discipline does not produce a forecast at the end. It produces a better-calibrated view of where the real market is and what it actually needs.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about a market your organization has decided it cannot yet enter because the forecast isn't ready. What does the forecast need to contain before it is ready? Most of the time the answer is: information that only real use can produce. Adoption rate estimates require people who have adopted. Use-case profiles require users who have used the product. Willingness-to-pay data requires buyers who have made a purchase decision. The forecast is waiting for information that the forecast process cannot generate. It is waiting for contact.

This is the discovery problem in its clearest form. An organization that requires forecast-level certainty before beginning contact is asking the market to supply, from a distance, information that only exists when someone is in the market. The requirement is not wrong as a goal. It is wrong as a sequence. Contact comes before clarity. Clarity does not come before contact. Requiring the sequence to run backward does not produce better information. It delays the point at which real information can arrive.

Anna's twelve commercial implant cases arrived with information the clinical protocol hadn't captured. The team was in contact with commercial users before they had a model for what commercial users would do. What those twelve cases surfaced (three use patterns outside the trial data) was not in any model the team had run. It arrived because the team was present when real use happened, not because the team had predicted it.

Chris's heritage speaker pilot was not in the original market plan. The team ran it because a community center asked. The usage patterns that came back, including the grammar module being skipped and the audio vocabulary section used at three times the standard rate, were not data the team had hypothesized. They were data that contact produced. If the team had required a market model for the heritage speaker segment before engaging, the model would have had nothing to build on.

The information that an emerging market needs to supply cannot be asked for before the market has formed. It can only be gathered by being in contact when the forming happens.

The practical implication is not to abandon planning. It is to reorder it. Plan the contact: what questions does the team need to answer, what use contexts will reveal those answers, what conditions will indicate that the opportunity is real or not real. Then make contact. Then build the forecast from what contact has produced, rather than making contact contingent on what forecasting has predicted.

The teams that enter with the clearest learning agenda are not the ones who had the best forecasts going in. They are the ones who knew exactly what questions they needed real use to answer. That precision about what to learn is itself a form of rigor. It is just not the kind that produces a clean number before anyone has set foot in the market.

examples.title: Anna's Review Surfaces Three Patterns Outside the Trial Protocol
examples.scenario: Twelve clinical folders are spread across the conference table, three with handwritten notes in the margins. Anna's weekly review was designed to track standard post-market outcomes: procedure time, adverse events, healing intervals. The notes in the margins are about something else. Patients in normal care settings are using the device in ways the clinical protocol never measured, not failures, but real-world applications that differ from trial conditions in three consistent patterns. The trial produced controlled data. The first twelve commercial cases are producing something else.
examples.whatToDo: Document the three patterns separately from the standard post-market outcomes report. The clinical trial produced controlled data. The commercial cases are producing discovery data that the trial protocol had no way to capture.
examples.whyItMatters: First commercial users apply a device in conditions the clinical trial did not anticipate. Real-world application generates information that controlled conditions exclude. Both types of data have value for different reasons.

examples.title: Chris's Pilot Data Does Not Match the Learner Model
examples.scenario: Looking back at the heritage speaker pilot, Chris can see that the team ran it because a community center requested access, not because the market model predicted a heritage speaker segment. The session data came back with patterns that did not match the learner model: the grammar module skipped, the audio vocabulary section used at three times the engagement rate of anything in the standard learner curriculum. Chris's market model had been built for formal foreign-language education settings. It had nothing to say about any of this.
examples.whatToDo: Document the heritage speaker usage patterns as a separate segment profile rather than discarding them as outside the learner model. The community center access request was a discovery entry point the market model had not generated.
examples.whyItMatters: A pilot run because an outside party requested access revealed a real but unmapped market segment. The discovery was not in the model because the model had no basis for predicting a use pattern that had not yet been observed.

examples.title: Lukas Opens the Second-Week Data and Finds Routes That Are Not on the Map
examples.scenario: At 7:45 a.m., Lukas opens the second-week data from the low-infrastructure city pilot. The demand model had flagged the city as a likely disqualification: minimal dedicated bike lanes, high automotive density, irregular street configuration. The commuter tracking data shows twenty-three riders using routes the model had not mapped: parking garage access paths, shared building corridors, a pedestrian bridge bypass. The routes are not on any cycling infrastructure map. The riders found them independently. Lukas is looking at commuter behavior the model said this city could not produce.
examples.whatToDo: Map the observed commuter routes before making the expansion decision. The model's disqualification was based on official infrastructure. The pilot data shows real use of routes the model had not included.
examples.whyItMatters: A city classified as a disqualification based on infrastructure data was producing real commuter behavior the model had not predicted. Contact with actual users in actual conditions revealed what the model could not.

examples.title: Isabel Predicts Underperformance and the Field Data Contradicts Her
examples.scenario: What happens when smallholder farmers apply a soil nutrient product at half the standard dose in two intervals instead of one? Isabel's trial data predicts suboptimal results based on protocol deviation. The field data from the pilot region is showing something else. Seventeen smallholders using hand-application logistics have adapted the dose timing to fit their plot access schedule. Their yield results are within five percent of the standard protocol results on comparable soil plots. Isabel predicted deviation from protocol would reduce results. The field data contradicts the prediction.
examples.whatToDo: Document the smallholder adaptation results as a separate evidence stream from the standard protocol. The protocol was built on large-farm logistics. The hand-application timing is a different use context worth tracking.
examples.whyItMatters: A use adaptation predicted to underperform produced comparable results. The smallholders were not failing to follow protocol. They were adapting to their conditions. That adaptation revealed a real use context the protocol had not modeled.

examples.title: Anders's Compliance Postmortem Contains Design Information Nobody Was Looking For
examples.scenario: The deployment site is a cleared lot in a flood-affected district, soft ground underfoot and an assembly crew that has never worked with the modular system. Anders's postmortem was conducted as a regulatory compliance exercise. The assembly challenges documented in the field, which connection sequences failed under non-standard conditions, which subcontractors could improvise, had never appeared in commercial deployments. The postmortem documented them because it was required to. The commercial design team read the report three months later.
examples.whatToDo: Route the assembly findings from the compliance postmortem to the commercial design team. The disaster deployment was not a market entry, but the stress conditions it created were real tests no commercial deployment had produced.
examples.whyItMatters: A compliance exercise produced design-relevant information that commercial deployments had not surfaced. The information was available because the organization was in contact with conditions outside its standard deployment context.

examples.title: Hiroshi's Team Reclassifies Five Edge-Case Tickets as a Market Signal
examples.scenario: You are reviewing the support ticket queue and five entries in the past two weeks are from the same category: gig platform operators using the scheduling module to assign contractors rather than employees. Before: Hiroshi's team routes these tickets to a lower support tier and marks them as non-standard use. After: the team interviews five gig platform operators and documents how they are using the scheduling module. The contractor assignment logic the module handles turns out to match the gig platform's actual workflow. The interviews confirm that it works.
examples.whatToDo: Conduct structured interviews with the five gig platform operators before reclassifying their tickets as non-standard. Their use pattern may be revealing a real market segment the product team had not modeled.
examples.whyItMatters: An edge-case support ticket turned out to be the signal of a real but unmapped market segment. Routing it to lower support without investigation would have treated a discovery opportunity as an anomaly.

questions.prompt: What makes forecasting an effective tool for mature markets but not for emerging ones?
choices: Mature markets have organized historical data on customers, purchase drivers, and competitive dynamics. Emerging markets lack this information, so forecasts must be built on inputs that do not yet exist.
Mature markets have better-informed leadership teams who make more accurate predictions because they have developed expertise in reading recurring competitive and customer patterns.

The team's track record on quantitative forecasts in adjacent markets has been worse than directional judgments from senior practitioners with deep customer relationships, which supports relying on qualitative judgment and direct stakeholder input at this stage.
questions.explanation: Forecasting is an exercise in organizing existing information. In mature markets that information is available. In emerging markets, the information a useful forecast would require is precisely the information that real contact with first users would generate.

questions.prompt: The medical device team's first twelve commercial implants produce use patterns outside the trial protocol. The team's post-market surveillance protocol has no category for unexpected use cases. What is the most important action?
choices: Report the unexpected use patterns as protocol deviations and flag them for corrective review, since the post-market surveillance protocol requires deviation documentation before the team can evaluate whether the pattern represents off-label use or a legitimate clinical application.

Wait until the pattern appears across a larger sample before entering it into the post-market report, so that the documentation reflects a statistically stable observation rather than a preliminary signal that may not persist as the commercial deployment expands.
Document the unexpected use patterns separately from the standard post-market outcomes and treat them as discovery data the trial protocol could not have captured.
questions.explanation: Commercial use generates real-world information that controlled trial conditions are designed to exclude. Unexpected use patterns in the first commercial deployments are discovery data, not anomalies to be corrected or deferred.

questions.prompt: A language-learning app's pilot with heritage speakers produces usage data that does not match the product's learner model. Heritage speakers skip foundational modules and use audio features at three times the standard rate. What should the product manager do?
choices: Redesign the heritage speaker flow as the primary use case, because the pilot data represents actual usage behavior and the product's learner model was built from assumptions about foreign-language study that the heritage speaker population does not share.
Document the heritage speaker usage pattern as a separate market segment profile rather than discarding it as an anomaly outside the learner model.

Terminate the heritage speaker pilot and direct future pilots to the originally modeled language-learner segment, treating the heritage speaker data as out-of-scope since the product's investment thesis was built around foreign-language acquisition rather than heritage language maintenance.
questions.explanation: Usage patterns that fall outside a product's current market model may be revealing a real but unmapped market segment. The data from the heritage speaker pilot should be documented as discovery data, not discarded because it didn't confirm the existing model.

questions.prompt: When the mobility startup's demand model flags a city as unsuitable because it lacks bike lane infrastructure, a pilot in that city produces stronger-than-modeled demand using informal routes. What should the startup do with the pilot data?
choices: Map the observed commuter routes separately from official infrastructure data and use the pilot contact data to revise the model's assumptions about what makes a city viable.

Terminate the pilot and exclude the city from future deployment consideration, because the demand model was validated against cities with established bike-lane infrastructure and the informal-route usage data cannot be interpreted without that baseline.

Update the demand model to include informal route density as an input variable alongside official bike-lane data, so that the model can distinguish between cities that lack infrastructure investment and cities that have developed informal route ecosystems through user behavior.
questions.explanation: The model's disqualification was based on data that did not include observed commuter behavior. The pilot produced real contact information. That information should update the model, not be rejected because it falls outside the model's current assumptions.

questions.prompt: A gig platform operator is using an HR software module to assign contractors rather than employees. The support team has classified this as non-standard use. What is the most discovery-appropriate response?
choices: Redesign the module's assignment logic to accommodate contractor classification before creating a documentation category for the usage pattern, so that the product team is not formalizing support for a workflow the module was not designed to handle reliably.

Continue routing gig platform support tickets to the lower-priority queue until the primary market segment is fully served, then reassess whether the contractor assignment pattern represents a deployment case worth investing in or a workaround that creates downstream liability.
Conduct structured interviews with the gig platform operators to document how they are using the module and whether the use reveals a real market segment the product team had not modeled.
questions.explanation: An unexpected use pattern in a support queue is a discovery opportunity. The team does not yet know whether the gig platform use represents a real market segment. Structured contact with the operators is the first step toward finding out.

questions.prompt: Why is a forecast-first, contact-second sequence a problematic approach for emerging markets?
choices: The firm's discovery process produces actionable intelligence from a 50-conversation sample that no historical-pattern analysis has matched in the past decade, which makes direct customer contact the more productive first step before any modeling begins.

Because the information a forecast of an emerging market requires, including customer data, purchase behavior, and competitive dynamics, is information that only real contact can produce. Requiring the forecast before contact demands the conclusion before the evidence.
Because forecasting is too expensive and time-consuming for early-stage market exploration, and the analytical resources required would be better allocated to direct customer engagement.
questions.explanation: A forecast in an emerging market must be built from information about customers, uses, and demand drivers. In an emerging market, that information does not yet exist in organized form. It is produced by contact with first users. Requiring the forecast before the contact is requiring the output before the input.

questions.prompt: The modular housing company's disaster-relief deployment produces assembly data that reveals assumptions in the commercial model that the commercial deployment had not generated. What does this reveal about discovery?
choices: Discovery opportunities arise only in commercial contexts designed explicitly for market research.

The operational extremes encountered in disaster deployments stress-test product assumptions that commercial deployments rarely reach, producing learning signals about structural limits of the assembly model that the commercial path cannot generate.
Discovery information can arrive through contact that was not planned as a discovery exercise. Being present in real use conditions generates information regardless of the team's intent.
questions.explanation: The modular housing team was not looking for design insights in the disaster deployment. The insights arrived because the team documented real assembly conditions. Discovery does not require a formal discovery exercise. It requires presence in real use conditions and a system for capturing what contact produces.

questions.prompt: A smallholder's non-protocol application of a soil nutrient product produces results comparable to the standard protocol on small plots. The product manager predicted this deviation would underperform. What does the comparable result reveal about the team's prior model?
choices: The team's model was built on large-farm application logistics and had no basis for predicting smallholder adaptation outcomes. The comparable result reveals a real use context the model had not included.
The team's protocol was poorly designed for field conditions and should be systematically replaced by the adapted smallholder approach as the new standard.
The comparable result was coincidental and likely reflects measurement variance rather than a genuinely valid adaptation, so it should not be used to update any part of the market model.
questions.explanation: The prediction of underperformance was locally correct for the standard application protocol. It was not designed to predict the outcome of a different use context. The comparable result reveals that a real use adaptation exists that the original model had not anticipated. Contact produced information the model could not.

questions.prompt: The product director argues that discovery-based market entry is inherently less rigorous than forecast-based entry because it lacks quantifiable predictions. How should this argument be assessed?
choices: The explicit prediction step that forecasting requires creates accountability that contact-based discovery lacks, which the firm's audit committee has been advocating for after recent failed bets on undocumented market assumptions.

The argument confuses the kind of rigor applied. Forecast-based entry applies rigor to existing data. Discovery-based entry applies rigor to learning questions and to what contact evidence will count. Both are disciplined approaches aimed at different stages of what is knowable.
The argument is wrong: forecasting provides no useful discipline in any market context and should be replaced by contact-based approaches in all stages of market development.
questions.explanation: Discovery is disciplined when organized around specific questions, defined evidence boundaries, and clear criteria for what will change the team's view. That is a different kind of discipline from forecasting, not an absence of discipline. Calling it less rigorous confuses the form of rigor with its absence.

reviewCards.front: An organization wants to enter an emerging market but requires a complete forecast first. Why does this requirement create a paradox?
reviewCards.back: Emerging markets lack the organized customer data, use-pattern evidence, and demand history that forecasting requires. The information a forecast needs is information that only real contact with first users can produce.

reviewCards.front: What does disciplined discovery mean, as distinct from undisciplined experimentation?
reviewCards.back: Disciplined discovery is organized around specific learning questions, defined evidence boundaries, and explicit criteria for what would change the team's current view of the opportunity. The discipline is aimed at learning, not at producing a forecast before contact.

reviewCards.front: A use pattern appears that does not match the product's current market model. Before classifying it as an anomaly, what question should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the unexpected use pattern might be revealing a real but unmapped market segment. An anomaly in the current model may be the first signal of a real customer population the model had not anticipated.

reviewCards.front: An organization requires a clear forecast before any market entry. What does this requirement produce in an emerging market?
reviewCards.back: It delays contact to the point where the forecast is waiting for information that only contact can supply. The sequence runs backward: the forecast requires the evidence, and the evidence requires the contact, and the contact is what is being postponed.

reviewCards.front: Your team insists on completing a forecast before making any contact with potential users in an emerging market. How should the entry sequence be reordered, and why?
reviewCards.back: Plan the contact before the forecast: define the learning questions, identify what use contexts will reveal answers, and set conditions for what would indicate a real opportunity. Make contact. Then build the forecast from what contact produced.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to treat the first stage of emerging market entry as a learning exercise organized around specific questions, rather than as a forecasting exercise that must be completed before contact can begin.

ifThenPlans.context: organization is delaying entry into a new market until the forecast is clearer
ifThenPlans.plan: If the team is waiting for forecast certainty, then identify the specific information the forecast needs that only real contact can produce. If that information is not available without contact, contact should precede forecasting, not follow it.

ifThenPlans.context: first users are using a product in ways outside the designed use case
ifThenPlans.plan: If unexpected use patterns appear in early deployment, then document them separately from standard post-market data and treat them as discovery data about real use contexts the market model did not anticipate.

ifThenPlans.context: a pilot produces results that contradict model predictions
ifThenPlans.plan: If pilot results contradict model predictions, then investigate whether the pilot population is using the product in a context the model did not include before concluding that the model is correct and the results are anomalous.

ifThenPlans.context: planning a first entry into an emerging market
ifThenPlans.plan: If the team is entering a market for the first time, then define the learning questions the entry needs to answer before designing the contact process. What does the team need to know about first users, use contexts, and performance attributes that only contact can reveal?

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one market your organization has decided it cannot enter yet because the forecast isn't clear enough. Write down one specific question, not a forecast but a concrete question, that real contact with potential users would let you answer within the next month.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when reviewing a market entry decision that is waiting for more information, identify the specific type of information it is waiting for and whether that information is available from analysis or requires contact with real users.

memorableLines.text: A model built on what you know cannot tell you what first users will teach you.
Discovery is disciplined. The discipline is aimed at learning, not forecasting.
The information that an emerging market needs to supply cannot be asked for before the market has formed. It can only be gathered by being in contact when the forming happens.

chapters.title: How to Appraise Your Organization's Capabilities and Disabilities
chapters.hook: What made you good at this work is not the same as what will make you good at that work.
chapters.counterintuition: The self-appraisal problem is not whether the organization has strong capabilities. The problem is that those capabilities were built to produce a specific kind of result in a specific context. When the context changes, the capability continues producing what it was designed to produce, which in fact may no longer be the right thing.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one organizational routine your team does exceptionally well. Write down the underlying assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then write one sentence about whether a new market you are considering shares that assumption.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Capabilities embed assumptions about what good work looks like. Fit appraisal asks whether the new context shares those assumptions. Strength in one setting can be an obstacle in another.

breakdown.fastRead:
Organizational capabilities are built to produce specific kinds of results in specific kinds of contexts. A pharmaceutical company's drug development process is excellent at producing safe, rigorously validated products because it was built to meet the standards that market requires. A legal firm's billable-hour discipline is excellent at ensuring that research quality is tracked and compensated because the billing model rewards it. These are real strengths. They are also routines: systematic ways of doing work that embed assumptions about what good outcomes look like.

When an organization enters a new context, those routines move with it. What does not automatically move is the match between what the routine produces and what the new context needs. A pharmaceutical process designed for eighteen-month iteration cycles arrives in a consumer wellness market where competitors iterate in three months. The process is just as good as it was. The context has different requirements.

A capability is context-dependent. What it enables in one setting, it may block in another.
breakdown.deepRead:
The self-appraisal problem is not a question of whether the organization has capable people or well-designed processes. Most organizations that are excellent at what they currently do have both. The problem is that capability is always relative to a task and a context. A capability that fits the current task precisely may not fit a new task at all, not because the capability degraded, but because it was built for a different set of requirements.

Routines are the most visible form of this. An organization's routines embed decisions about what matters: how quickly outputs need to be produced, what quality standards apply, what a successful outcome looks like to the customer who will use it. Those decisions were made, consciously or not, in response to the requirements of the current market. The routine optimizes for what the current market rewards. It is not designed to re-evaluate that optimization when the market changes.

The routine has not failed. The context has changed.

What makes this difficult is that the same routine that is an obstacle in the new context is a strength in the existing one. Removing it to enter the new context would degrade performance in the place where it is working. Keeping it blocks entry into the place where it is not. The appraisal question is not 'is this capability good?' The appraisal question is: does this capability fit what the new task specifically requires?
breakdown.fullRead:
Think of one thing your organization does exceptionally well. Not a general attribute: a specific routine or process. How long does it take to validate a new product claim? How many approvals does a customer communication go through before it ships? What is the standard for how a recommendation gets written and presented? These routines produce outcomes your organization values, which is why they exist. They were built to produce those outcomes reliably.

Now think about what assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. The validation timeline assumes that accuracy is worth the time it takes. The approval process assumes that the risk of miscommunication exceeds the cost of delay. The recommendation standard assumes that the work will be handed off rather than owned. These assumptions are embedded so deeply that the routine does not surface them as assumptions. They are simply how things get done. Ask why the validation takes as long as it does, and the answer is: because that is the standard. The standard does not explain itself. It was formed in a context that no longer needs explaining.

When that routine moves into a new context, the assumption moves with it. A new context may have a different view of what accuracy is worth, what delay costs, or who owns the output. If it does, the routine will produce exactly what it was designed to produce, and the new context will treat that output as a performance problem rather than a quality signal. The routine is not broken. It is producing what it was built to produce. The problem is that the new context has different requirements.

Kathryn's automation platform arrived in a firm whose billable-hour culture treated research efficiency as a problem rather than an asset. The platform was good. The firm's discipline was real. The assumption that high-quality work requires time investment was embedded in every associate's understanding of what they were being paid to produce. The platform could not change that assumption. The capability mismatch was not visible in any performance metric. It was visible in the utilization log.

The question is not whether the organization is capable. It is whether the capability fits the task.

Fit appraisal requires naming the assumption before assessing the capability. What does this routine optimize for? What does the new task require? If those two answers are the same, the capability is likely to transfer. If they are different, the capability that looks like a strength in the existing context is likely to produce the obstacle in the new one. That is not a critique of the capability. It is an observation about where it was built to work.

examples.title: Kathryn's Platform Dashboard Shows 22 Percent Utilization
examples.scenario: "Why are the associates still spending three hours on cases the platform should answer in thirty minutes?" the senior partner asks. Kathryn looks at the platform utilization dashboard: 22 percent active use across the associate pool. The platform is working. The research it generates is accurate. The associates are accurate too, and they are producing more billable hours by doing research the slow way. The billing model rewards thorough, time-documented work. The platform's efficiency benefit is a reduction in the metric the culture is built to protect.
examples.whatToDo: Identify whether the billing model needs to change before the platform can produce its intended benefit. The utilization problem is not a technology problem. The billing structure rewards the behavior the platform is designed to replace.
examples.whyItMatters: A platform that reduces research time reduces billable hours under the current billing model. The culture built around billable-hour excellence is the obstacle to the efficiency the platform offers. Both are real. They are incompatible.

examples.title: Thomas's Supplement Line Arrives After Competitors Have Set the Price Point
examples.scenario: Looking back at the wellness supplement launch timeline, Thomas can trace every delay to a process doing its job correctly. The safety review was thorough. The regulatory documentation was complete. The quality testing met pharmaceutical standards. Consumer wellness competitors who arrived nine months earlier had a shorter version of each review and were iterating on customer feedback while Thomas's team completed its third compliance cycle. The product reached market with better documentation than any competitor's and arrived after they had already set the price point.
examples.whatToDo: Map the pharmaceutical process timeline against competitor iteration speed before applying it to the next product. The process fits pharmaceutical standards. It may not fit the consumer market's competitive tempo.
examples.whyItMatters: A development process built for pharmaceutical precision produces pharmaceutical timing. Consumer wellness competitors iterate faster. The process produces excellent quality and creates a competitive timing obstacle. Both are true.

examples.title: Hugo's Charging Network App Prototype Meets the Dealer Agreement Clause
examples.scenario: At 9:00 a.m., Hugo opens the EV charging network app prototype alongside the dealer agreement's clause on consumer data ownership. The prototype requires direct consumer registration, usage history, and payment processing. The dealer agreement assigns consumer data rights to dealer franchisees, not to the OEM. Hugo's team has spent four months building a direct driver relationship into an application that the dealer network agreement prohibits. The decision is now structural, not technical.
examples.whatToDo: Identify whether a structural arrangement exists that captures the direct consumer relationship requirement without violating the dealer agreement's terms before building further into the current structure.
examples.whyItMatters: A dealer network is a real competitive asset and a set of agreements that define how the OEM can relate to consumers. In a market requiring direct consumer data, those agreements prohibit the capability the new service requires.

examples.title: Petra's Newsletter Is the Most Rigorously Sourced and the Slowest
examples.scenario: What does a broadcast journalist with thirty years of source relationships and a multi-source verification standard bring to newsletter journalism? Petra's newsletter has the most rigorously sourced content in its category. It also publishes two days after competitors have already set the story. Her verification standard requires three independent source confirmations. By the time she has the third, the story has moved. Petra predicted her sourcing network would be a competitive advantage. Subscriber growth is going to the faster writers.
examples.whatToDo: Define what accuracy standard the newsletter's readers require before applying the broadcast verification cadence. The broadcast and newsletter formats have different speed-accuracy trade-offs. The standard should fit the format.
examples.whyItMatters: A verification standard built for broadcast journalism produces broadcast-quality content on a broadcast timeline. In a format where recency matters, that timeline is a competitive disadvantage. The strength is real. The fit is not.

examples.title: Diego's All-Hands Deck Is Forty Slides and Nobody Owns Slide 28
examples.scenario: The all-hands deck is forty slides, each section argued with data and a recommendation on the last page. Diego has delivered presentations like this for eleven years. The software company's team is asking who implements slide 28. His postmortem on the first six months shows excellent analysis quality and precise recommendations. Every recommendation was written for handoff rather than ownership: framed for an executive who would assign the work, not for the person doing it the next morning.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the next recommendation as an implementation plan with named owners before presenting it. The analytical quality is not the problem. The deliverable structure is optimized for handoff, not for the person who owns the execution.
examples.whyItMatters: A consulting deliverable is built for handoff. An operational plan is built for ownership. The same analytical quality produces a different kind of document depending on which context it is written for.

examples.title: Layla's Custom Details Are the Factory's Variance Problem
examples.scenario: You are walking through Layla's studio portfolio: twelve residential commissions with site-specific solutions that no two look the same. Before: Layla applies the same custom-optimization discipline to the modular housing design. Each unit has a site-specific structural decision and a custom facade detail. After: the manufacturing partner's review marks fifteen variance flags across the first design package. Every custom decision is a production deviation. The studio's competitive strength is the factory's most significant production problem.
examples.whatToDo: Identify which design decisions can be standardized before the next design package. The studio's discipline produces excellent bespoke work. Manufacturing requires repeatable precision, which is a different definition of quality.
examples.whyItMatters: Bespoke design and manufacturing have different definitions of quality. A studio that optimized for differentiation will generate the factory's variance problems. Both sides are correct within their own definition.

questions.prompt: What makes an organizational capability context-dependent rather than universally applicable?
choices: Capabilities are context-dependent only because organizations are too large to change quickly, and this limitation disappears when organizations build internal agility mechanisms or reduce bureaucratic layers.

A capability was built to produce a specific kind of result in a specific context. It embeds assumptions about what a good outcome looks like. When the context changes, those assumptions may not match the new requirements.
Context-dependence applies only to process capabilities, not to individual people capabilities, since individuals can adapt to new environments through training and professional development.
questions.explanation: Organizational capabilities are not abstract strengths. They are routines and processes built to produce specific results in specific conditions. The conditions those capabilities were built for may not apply in a new context, even if the capabilities themselves remain strong.

questions.prompt: When a pharmaceutical company applies its drug development governance process to a consumer wellness supplement line, the process imposes 18-month approval timelines for formulation changes that competitors approve in three weeks. What does this reveal?
choices: The pharmaceutical division lacked sufficient motivation and competitive awareness to adjust its development timeline for the consumer wellness market, despite having the underlying technical capabilities.

The consumer wellness market requires drug-level validation standards, which the company correctly applied because consumer health products and pharmaceuticals share the same fundamental safety obligations.

The drug development process embeds an assumption that iteration speed is worth sacrificing for thoroughness. The consumer wellness market rewards iteration speed above the thoroughness level the pharmaceutical process provides.
questions.explanation: The pharmaceutical process is not wrong for the pharmaceutical market. It embeds an assumption about what quality requires. The consumer wellness market embeds a different assumption. The process transferred. The assumption mismatch did not resolve.

questions.prompt: The senior broadcast journalist applies her multi-source verification standard to a newsletter. Her newsletter consistently misses breaking stories but publishes pieces that hold up to scrutiny. Which question does this situation raise about the journalist's capability?
choices: The verification standard was built for broadcast accuracy requirements. Newsletter readers reward recency at a different speed threshold. The same standard that produces authoritative broadcast journalism produces slow newsletter content.
Her verification standard is too rigorous for any journalism context and should be reduced across all reporting formats to enable faster publication and audience engagement.
The outcome reveals that she has insufficient sources for the newsletter journalism format specifically, and she should develop a dedicated source network suited to faster publication cycles.
questions.explanation: Multi-source verification is not wrong as a journalism standard. It embeds an assumption about what accuracy requires and what delay is acceptable. The newsletter context has a different speed-accuracy trade-off than broadcast journalism. The standard transferred. The fit did not.

questions.prompt: The consulting partner takes a COO role at a 30-person software company. Six months in, her recommendations are analytically sound but operationally misaligned with the resource level the company can support. What does this suggest about her consulting capability in this context?
choices: She lacks the analytical depth and operational experience needed to run a software company, and the COO role requires a fundamentally different orientation toward ownership and execution than consulting has developed in her.

Consulting excellence requires polished deliverables built for handoff. COO work requires owning and revising the output in real time. The same deliverable quality that distinguishes a consulting engagement signals the wrong relationship to ownership in an operational role.

The company's team is not capable of executing the recommendations she provides, and the organization needs to hire additional operational staff who can implement complex strategic initiatives without requiring detailed handoff documentation.
questions.explanation: The consultant's analytical and communication capabilities are genuine strengths. They were built for a context where the deliverable is handed to a client who implements it. In an operational role, the output must be built to be owned and revised. The capability exists. The assumption about who owns the output does not fit.
